    • As a flag carrier of the 3rd most populous nation in South America, I went into my Aerolíneas Argentinas flight with them at the start of the year expecting some pretty standard things: enjoying my SkyTeam benefits, lounge access, and, most importantly of all for someone living out of a suitcase, checked bag allowance.
    • However, I quickly discovered that the airline is basically an ultra-low-cost airline masquerading as a full-service carrier.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    This might seem like a rather niche topic to cover in my first week at OMAAT, but after Ben mentioned this story in his intro article, I thought it made sense to follow up fast with an explainer.

    As a flag carrier of the 3rd most populous nation in South America, I went into my Aerolíneas Argentinas flight with them at the start of the year expecting some pretty standard things: enjoying my SkyTeam benefits, lounge access, and, most importantly of all for someone living out of a suitcase, checked bag allowance.

    However, I quickly discovered that the airline is basically an ultra-low-cost airline masquerading as a full-service carrier.

    I needed to get from Buenos Aires to Mendoza for a friend’s 40th birthday celebrations. Options were pretty limited, with nonstop flights available with either JetSmart or, indeed, Aerolíneas Argentinas. I try to avoid low-cost airlines when possible, because, quite simply, I enjoy the flying experience, and low-cost airlines tend to suck every enjoyable element out of it.

    Other pros to booking Aerolíneas Argentinas, personally:.

    After researching my options, I used Flying Blue miles to book two single tickets from Buenos Aires Jorge Newbery Aeroparque Airport (AEP) to Mendoza’s El Plumerillo Airport (MDZ).

    I can’t remember how much the fares were when I was planning the trip, but each one-way flight cost a total of 7,500 miles and less than $10 in taxes and fees.

    Looking now at example fares for January next year, round-trips for Aerolíneas’ lowest and most restrictive fare category (more on that to come) start at around $120.

    Sources indicate that I know it’s not a hard-and-fast rule, but I’ve come to expect that, most of the time, the baggage allowance listed on the booking confirmation is correct. This is often true with redemptions, such as British Airways, which notably offers and acknowledges a 23 kg baggage allowance when redeeming Avios, even for a short-haul flight in economy.

    The confirmation email I received clearly noted 1x checked bag with a 23 kg limit.

    Again, the attached PDF stated that I’d have 1x checked bag included.

    It has been revealed that as the Argentinian scamsters would have it, I learned at check-in that the airline has a 15 kg weight limit for checked bags on domestic flights. I tried to plead my case and indicated the rather unhelpful check-in agent my booking confirmation, but he basically noted, “that means nothing.”.

    So they weigh your bag, give you a ticket, and then you have to exit the terminal building and find this little cashier where they collect their scammy little earnings. And what better place to proudly display a “SkyTeam Alliance Member” sign at the very desk where the airline also proudly collects baggage fees from SkyTeam elite status holders, even when traveling on award tickets?

    It has been revealed that once I’d been charged the fee of around $17, I had to join another queue back inside and show them I’d paid for the extra weight before they’d dispatch my bag. You might look at the $32 in fees I paid and think, “What is he complaining about?” But this isn’t about the actual amount of money; it’s the principle.

    In a recent development, only after the debacle did I learn the extent of Aerolíneas Argentinas’ domestic fare restrictions. Imagine paying $510 (more than four times the cheapest fare) for a “premium economy” ticket and still only getting 15 kg checked baggage allowance, no Fast Pass, no priority boarding (what?), and no lounge access. The latter isn’t such a big deal as Aerolíneas Argentinas doesn’t even have its own lounge at AEP.

    Airline loyalty is really important to me, and I generally value it more than the ability to redeem miles. Maybe I’ll get into that another day….

    Things got off to a fairly normal start when I saw the Sky Priority check-in kiosks at Aeroparque.

    That feeling of normalcy lasted as long as it took me to get from the sign to the aforementioned conversation about the checked bag situation at the desk. Despite my very best efforts combining my Castilian Spanish and Geordie charm (we’re called Geordies where I’m from in the North East of England), the man at the check-in desk seemed to take real pleasure in explaining that the checked bag rules on my booking confirmation were irrelevant and I’d have to pay the fee.

    For what it’s worth, Sky Priority check-in was also available at Mendoza.

    Being nickel-and-dimed for a checked bag by a flag carrier airline is shameful.

    It has been revealed that back at Aeroparque, there was no fast track, and the security line was ridiculously long. That mentioned, it’s rare in South America to have fast track lanes. For example, no matter whether you’re flying economy or first class (even Air France La Première), everyone waits in the same line to clear pre-departure passport control at São Paulo’s Guarulhos.

    Thanks to my Priority Pass, I did have access to the surprisingly nice AMAE lounge in the national departures part of the airport.

    Recent findings suggest that even from the outside, my 15-year-old Embraer 190 looked like it had seen better days. The zebra-striped dirt streaks running from each window suggested this place hadn’t been washed or hit the maintenance hangar for a while.

    Inside the Embraer, however, could have been a lot worse. The older seats had thick padding, and despite being a small 2-2-configured cabin, it felt bright and spacious.

    It was the Uber advertising on every single headrest that I found most jarring.

    In a recent development, the legroom was decent, too. The retro seatback screens, on the other hand, were pretty much redundant.

    It was stepping on board the 16-year-old Boeing 737-700 back to Buenos Aires that Aerolíneas Argentinas’ low-costness was most glaring. Looking at this, I would never guess this plane belonged to a flag carrier. The seats were very uncomfortable, and I think I remember they didn’t recline either.

    As for service, I don’t recall it being particularly good or particularly bad. Forgettable is probably the most accurate word.

    Imagine the likes of Spirit (RIP) or Ryanair calling itself a national flag carrier; that’s basically what Aerolíneas Argentinas is. I’m planning a trip with my dad and brother for February next year that includes Argentina, and I will actively avoid flying Aerolíneas, even if it means forgoing the chance to earn any Flying Blue miles and XPs.

    It has been revealed that it’s almost as if the airline has been abandoned. After all, the only real competition is low-cost airlines at LATAM — the full-service carrier which dominates South America. Who knows, maybe things will change come 2028 when it takes delivery of upcoming Airbus A330-900s and Boeing 737 MAXs.

    If I were a power that be at SkyTeam, I’d definitely remove the airline from the alliance. And if I had my way, Aerolíneas Argentinas would be bought by LATAM, and the cherry on top would be LATAM joining SkyTeam. I should probably put a business case together for that….

    Recent findings suggest that best thing about them: Their livery. Stunning!. In person even better.

    Sources indicate that I flew from GRU to LHR on BA in about 2018, first class redemption. I don't remember a long passport queue, but I do remember that I was escorted by the check-in agent from the desk to the lounge which I found surprising, but could explain the lack of problems.     💡 Key Takeaways
    • A new deal with Miami-Dade County will help American Airlines solidify and eventually expand its maintenance operations at Miami International Airport.
    • The county revealed this week that it will buy a hangar and maintenance space at Miami International from a third-party owner and lease it directly to American for its MRO operations.
    • According to the Miami Herald, American already leases the property and uses it for maintenance work, but a change in ownership from private jet operator Aero Miami to the county will give American more leeway to develop the space as it sees fit.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A new deal with Miami-Dade County will help American Airlines solidify and eventually expand its maintenance operations at Miami International Airport.

    The county revealed this week that it will buy a hangar and maintenance space at Miami International from a third-party owner and lease it directly to American for its MRO operations. The acquisition includes Hangar 890, Building 891, 10.2 acres of land, and a 2.2-acre parking lot.

    According to the Miami Herald, American already leases the property and uses it for maintenance work, but a change in ownership from private jet operator Aero Miami to the county will give American more leeway to develop the space as it sees fit. The fresh lease with the county will run for 20 years and cost American $67.8 million, the newspaper noted.

    Sources indicate that the airline intends to keep more than 650 aircraft maintenance workers at the facility. It has also agreed to complete about $13.9 million in building repairs.

    “Miami is a cornerstone of American’s international network and a consequential part of our long-term growth strategy,” American Senior Vice President of Miami Operations Juan Carlos Liscano stated in a news release. “This agreement reinforces our dedication to our Miami team and preserves our ability to continue growing our network to more destinations around the world for our customers.”.

    American is the largest airline at Miami, carrying more than half of all passengers there.

    His graduate work concentrated on Global and National Security, Low-Intensity Conflict, Modern Warfare, and US grand strategy. He also undertook extensive regional studies, analyzing how key regions integrate into the broader US security architecture.

    This rigorous program provided him with a comprehensive understanding of U.S. military operations, global strategy, and weapons systems. Additionally, he gained a strong appreciation for great power competition.—an increasingly central force shaping international relations and conflict for the foreseeable future.

    The aviation industry depends on far more than pilots and cabin crew to keep its aircraft flying and its global operations running smoothly. Behind every departure is a network of highly skilled professionals responsible for flight planning, aircraft maintenance, complex electronic systems, engineering, and the financial decisions that keep airlines competitive. Many of these essential roles take place well away from the passenger cabin, yet they offer rewarding career opportunities and considerable earning potential.

    Industry observers note that from FAA-certificated aircraft dispatchers and experienced maintenance technicians to avionics specialists, aerospace engineers, and airline revenue analysts, these professionals bring specialized knowledge to one of the world's most demanding industries. Here are five aviation careers that offer attractive salaries without requiring individuals to become pilots.

    Industry observers note that airlines must do more than fill seats to remain profitable. Behind the ticket prices passengers see when booking a flight is a team of revenue management and pricing analysts, whose job is to determine how much an airline should charge for each seat and when. These professionals study passenger demand, booking trends, competitor fares, and historical sales data to help airlines maximize revenue across their networks.

    According to JetBlue Airways, its revenue management team is responsible for maximizing ticket revenue on every flight, with analysts working across two main areas: pricing and yield management. Pricing analysts monitor competitor fares and adjust the airline's own pricing strategies, while yield analysts manage seat availability and fare levels to make the most of passenger demand. American Airlines similarly describes the role as using data-driven pricing and inventory strategies to improve revenue performance across assigned markets.

    The work is highly analytical and generally requires a degree in finance, economics, business, mathematics, or a related field, alongside strong data analysis skills. JetBlue lists a salary range of $58,000 to $86,000 (£44,200 to £65,700) for its Associate Analyst Revenue Management position, while ZipRecruiter lists airline revenue management analyst salaries across a range of current vacancies.

    An aircraft dispatcher is an FAA-certificated airline operations professional. These individuals are closely involved in the planning, releasing, monitoring, and continual support of flights during ground, in-air, and arrival operations. GlassDoor states that these aviation professionals earn between $73,000 (£55.500) and $137,000 (£104,200K) per year.

    It has been revealed that adding to this, Thrust Flight School says that their salary primarily depends on the airline they work for and how many years of service they have under their belt. They state that first-year pay at most regional carriers is between $41,000 (£31,200) and $52,000 (£39,600) a year. However, major US airlines will pay a first-year airline dispatcher approximately $95,000 (£72,300), with the top of the pay scale reaching around $170,000 (£129,300) for an 11-year veteran.

    According to the US Aviation Academy, "the dispatcher and pilot in command share defined responsibility for preflight planning, delay, and dispatch release." Additionally, a dispatcher "monitors each assigned flight, provides information needed for safety, and participates in cancellation or redispatch decisions when a flight cannot safely operate or continue as planned.".

    A Typical Workday For a Dispatcher.

    Reviews relevant weather, NOTAMs, operational complications, aircraft information, and flights assigned to the desk.

    Evaluates route, fuel, weather, alternates, aircraft information, and other dispatch requirements.

    Tracks several assigned flights and watches for information or conditions that may affect their safe operation.

    Exchanges operational information with flight crews and coordinates with other airline operational resources as required.

    Evaluates weather, airport, routing, aircraft, or other changes and helps determine the applicable operational response.

    Transfers relevant information about active flights and operational concerns when responsibilities move to another qualified dispatcher.

    Generally, dispatchers perform their work in centralized airline operations environments rather than airport control towers. Airlines use different terms for the areas in which they work, including Operations Control Centers (OCCs), System Operations Control Centers (SOCCs), and Network Operations Centers.

    In a recent development, to grasp the scale of the daily operations managed by dispatchers, American Airlines, generally considered the largest airline in the United States, notes that it maintains a staff of 600 dispatchers and operations specialists. American states that it operates "6,000 daily flights to more than 350 destinations in more than 60 countries," with its dispatchers playing an integral role in supporting these global operations.

    Industry observers note that flight safety involves numerous overlapping and interconnected layers of responsibility, expertise, security, and regulation. A crucial component of the aviation ecosystem is the generally unseen aircraft mechanic. USAFacts explains that the oft-stated expression "flying is safer than driving" is absolutely valid. The site states that in "2023, 33 plane passengers were injured over 773 billion miles of air travel. Put another way, you could circle the globe over 940,000 times for every one airplane injury.".

    In a recent development, this level of consistent safety depends a great deal on the skill, proficiency, and training of aircraft mechanics, as well as their continual learning and honing of their skills. These professionals ensure that every aircraft, from nose to tail and fuselage top to wheel, is rigorously inspected, repaired, and cleared for flight.

    For their essential services and expertise, US Aviation Academy reports that the median annual salary for an aircraft mechanic was $79,870 in May 2025. Further, they add that the mean annual wage was $84,740 (£64,742), while the median hourly wage was $38.40 (£29.34). The bottom 10% of this skill pool earned less than $48,780 (£37,263), while the highest 10% earned more than $128,890 (£98,498).

    Recent findings suggest that while the pay for this line of work is rewarding, North America is facing a growing shortage of aviation maintenance personnel. The Aviation Technician Education Council reports that there is a widening deficit of certificated aircraft mechanics, which is expected to increase from approximately 9,100 this year to 20,000 by 2030, representing 12% of anticipated demand. Fortunately, the Council reports that the FAA issued 11,103 new mechanic certificates in 2025, 23.2% more than in 2024 and the highest annual total since the agency began publishing the data.

    Industry observers note that on a daily basis, major airlines entrust their $306 million to $442 million (£234 million to £338 million) Boeing 777s (or similar aircraft) to the capable hands of their avionics technicians. These men and women install navigation, radio, radar, and autopilot systems. They also repair or replace faulty wiring, sensors, and instrument panels, and carry out post-repair testing.

    It has been revealed that one miswired transponder or uncalibrated altimeter can render an aircraft unfit to fly or affect crucial systems while airborne. Modern passenger jets are equipped with hundreds of interconnected electronic components, and a failure in one can potentially affect others. Like maintenance technicians, their counterparts in avionics require a great deal of training, usually 18 to 24 months. Their courses cover circuit analysis, digital electronics, and the proper use of diagnostic equipment.

    It has been revealed that upon completion, the US Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) states that these skilled workers earn a median annual wage of $82,280 (£62,862), based on 2025 statistics. Further, the BLS reports that there were approximately 19,800 avionics technicians employed in the US in 2025, and the future outlook for this profession is encouraging.

    Sources indicate that to this point, the Bureau notes that employment among avionics technicians is projected to grow by 9% between 2025 and 2035. It also projects about "13,100 openings for aircraft and avionics equipment mechanics and technicians. . .projected each year, on average, over the decade. Many of those openings are expected to result from the need to replace workers who transfer to different occupations or exit the labor force, such as to retire.".

    When we watch an aircraft fly overhead, land at an airport, or enter the cabin, everything we look at and touch has been meticulously designed with ergonomics, functionality, mechanical integrity, and comfort in mind. Those behind this specialized planning are aeronautics engineers.

    According to recent reports, these men and women earn a median annual salary of $134,960 (£103,126), according to the BLS. Employment in this field is projected to grow by 8% between 2025 and 2035, with approximately 3,800 openings across the industry each year over the decade. Many of these openings are likely to result from the need to replace engineers who transfer to different occupations or retire.

    The Museum of Flight states that there are five types of engineers within the field of aviation who contribute to the design, manufacture, and support of aircraft. These include industrial, structural, avionics, acoustics, and sales engineers. Each brings a different area of expertise to the industry, from improving manufacturing processes and ensuring structural integrity to developing complex electronic systems and reducing aircraft noise. Together, these specialists help ensure that modern aircraft are not only capable of flying safely but are also efficient, functional, and commercially viable.

    Recent findings suggest that industrial engineers initiative and improve how aircraft are manufactured, ensuring they are produced as efficiently and safely as possible. Structural engineers design the frame of an aircraft, making sure it is structurally sound enough to withstand the rigors of not only flight but also harsh landings and taxiing. Avionics engineers map out the electrical systems that span the aircraft, from the cockpit to the tail. Finally, acoustics engineers use testing to identify ways to reduce noise inside and outside an aircraft. Sales engineers, meanwhile, work directly with customers, explaining aircraft capabilities and helping airlines, governments, and other buyers select aircraft that meet their operational requirements.

    Beginner’s luck: Freshmen leave it to chance at House office lottery

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (925 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that rep.-elect Mark Teixeira reacts after drawing the worst chip during Tuesday’s lottery for newly elected members of Congress.
    • As far as birthdays go, Rep.-elect Shannon Taylor was having a pretty good one.
    • Crowded into a room in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday morning with the rest of her freshman class, the Virginia Democrat walked up to a table with a wooden box and reached in.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that rep.-elect Mark Teixeira reacts after drawing the worst chip during Tuesday’s lottery for newly elected members of Congress. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    As far as birthdays go, Rep.-elect Shannon Taylor was having a pretty good one.

    Crowded into a room in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday morning with the rest of her freshman class, the Virginia Democrat walked up to a table with a wooden box and reached in.

    “This is so nervewracking,” she said, before pulling out a chip with a “1” printed on it.

    Her prize was a coveted one — first choice of office space. Every two years, incoming members of the House play a game of chance to see who can land the best real estate and who will be relegated to less desirable corners of the Capitol complex.

    The room broke out in raucous applause and a standing ovation. Her latest colleagues started singing “Happy Birthday.”.

    Sources indicate that not everyone was so lucky. Rep.-elect Mark Teixeira, R-Texas, pulled number 105 — the very last one. The former MLB player raised his arms in a mock celebration.

    “Lets all hope for the luck of the Taylors,” noted Rep.-elect Brent Taylor, R-Tenn., only to emerge with number 81.

    The newly-elected members got their turn in a random order, walking up one by one to a table where deputy executive director of House Office Buildings Kornell Rancy kept watch over the box of chips.

    It has been revealed that rep.-elect John Cowan, R-Ga., was the first to pick a number. The first neurosurgeon to be elected to Congress, Cowan wore his white doctor’s coat as he pulled number 11 out of the box.

    “I wanted to do something where I’m just representing health care providers around the country,” Cowan said.

    According to recent reports, as returning members lay claim to more desirable offices made available by those who resign, retire or lose elections, the space they’ve abandoned is left for the newcomers, who are on the Hill this week for orientation. Many of them will end up in the Longworth Building, where suites can be awkward or cramped.

    Recent findings suggest that not all offices are created equal, and the calculus has changed over the years. The previously undesirable Cannon Building just underwent a budget-busting renovation that lasted more than a decade, with a spacious courtyard opening earlier this year. But the coveted Rayburn Building still retains its prestige, despite repeated and dire warnings from the Architect of the Capitol about its crumbling infrastructure.

    “You’re welcome,” mentioned Rep.-elect Amish Shah, D-Ariz., after pulling a disappointing number 94.

    Prior to the lottery, Rep.-elect Trever Nehls, R-Texas, was hoping for the best but had a backup plan in case his number stated otherwise.

    It has been revealed that “If I don’t pick number one, I’m going to offer one of these cigars as a trade to whoever gets it,” he said, pointing to three of them sticking out of his jacket pocket. He’s preparing to take over the seat right now held by his twin brother Troy, who shares a fondness for stogies.

    The office space lottery dates back to 1908, when members of the 60th Congress received their first office assignments after the completion of what would be named the Cannon Building. A House page drew names and numbers from a box, and members selected their offices from a chart, according to House Office Buildings executive director of facility operations Joe Yates, who kicked things off Tuesday with a history lesson.

    The lottery now is a little more modern, with members poring over virtual office layouts and doing walkthroughs of spaces on laptops.

    In a recent development, “If somebody had to get 105, I’m glad it was me because I am here to serve, and I’m serving my freshman class by picking the worst office,” Teixeira remarked. “This is low on my priority list.”.

    Some members announced their lucky draws themselves, while others let Yates break the news.

    “Come visit me,” said Rep.-elect Chris Gober, R-Texas, after pulling number 2 from the box.

    After the lottery itself, members huddled with their staff to strategize about the next steps — how to leverage their numbers and select the best suites left on the list, while also exploring layouts, paint colors and carpeting.

    “First and foremost, a good layout, so we can do good work, and people can be comfortable in doing the work, and then a convenient location. Very utilitarian,” stated Rep.-elect Scott Wiener, D-Calif., of his priorities.

    It has been revealed that “We’ll get a decent Longworth office,” said Wiener, who drew pick 43. “Cannon would have been ideal, but I’m happy with any office.”.

    Industry observers note that rep.-elect Manny Rutinel, D-Colo., was hoping to replicate the good luck of some of his colleagues. “I’m going to do the Shannon Taylor and Sam Forstag. It’s eyes closed, behind the back,” he noted of his moves, reaching into the box. But it wasn’t enough, and Rutinel pulled number 69.

    According to recent reports, “These are not red numbers, these are not blue numbers. These are the remaining numbers, and there ain’t that many,” noted Rep.-elect Johnny Garcia, D-Texas, who was among the last few people to pick. He emerged with number 75.

    And when Rep.-elect Joe Strada, R-Fla., the last of the incoming members to draw, walked up to the table, the whole room cheered.

    “Wouldn’t it be crazy if I picked number 1?” he joked, pulling out the last chip in the box.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    American Airlines has just officially “retired” its Flagship First product on the Boeing 777-300ER, meaning that no US carrier offers an international first class product anymore. The good news is that an updated business class product is in the process of being rolled out, and that’s something that should benefit a lot of travelers.

    As I’ve covered in the past, American is in the process of eliminating its “premium” first class product, and that change was just implemented for flights as of this week on the carrier’s biggest planes.

    Specifically, the Boeing 777-300ER is American’s “flagship” aircraft, with 20 of the planes in the fleet. As of this week, the airline is no longer selling first class on these planes. Now, plenty of 777-300ERs with these cabins are still flying around, as American has just started reconfiguring its 777-300ERs with upcoming cabins, including the new business class.

    It has been revealed that still, for flights effective immediately, first class seats are just being sold as standard business class seats, and any business class passenger can select seats in the first two rows (you’d think they’d try to charge extra or at least reserve them for select elite members, but nope). So there will no longer be a differentiated soft product… not that there was much of a difference as of late anyway!

    With this change, no US carrier offers an international first class product anymore either, so it very much is the end of an era. American’s 777 first class seats were controversial — on the one hand, I kind of love how they swivel, though on the other hand, they really lack privacy, and the soft product left a lot to be desired.

    Industry observers note that I expect we’ll continue to see these planes flying around well into late 2027, or possibly even into 2028, depending on how fast the retrofit project happens. American’s dedicated first class ground product has also largely been discontinued, as Flagship First Dining has turned into Flagship Dining, so a la carte lounge dining is now available to eligible business class passengers as well.

    It’s great that these planes will be getting latest business class suites, as they’ll also be the aircraft belonging to a US carrier with the most business class seats, as they’ll have 70 of them… that’s lot!

    While American has now eliminated its international first class product, it’s worth emphasizing that the airline still technically has a “premium” first class, in the sense of a cabin above business class.

    Industry observers note that specifically, American still has its specially configured Airbus A321T aircraft, which are used primarily for flights between Newly introduced York (JFK) and Los Angeles (LAX) and San Francisco (SFO). The planes have 10 reverse herringbone seats spread across five rows, in a 1-1 configuration.

    American also plans to eliminate this product, as the A321Ts will be reconfigured into standard A321 domestic configuration aircraft, and A321XLRs will be taking over the transcon routes.

    American has stopped selling first class on these planes for flights as of March 28, 2027. After that date we’ll still see some of the planes flying with the cabins, but the first class seats will simply be sold as business class.

    American Airlines has officially eliminated its international first class product, as Boeing 777-300ERs no longer have Flagship First for sale. These planes are being retrofitted, as first class seats are being eliminated, and newly introduced business class suites are being introduced. However, the planes will keep flying around with the current cabins for quite some time, and business class passengers can freely assign the first class seats.

    In the spring, we’ll see American eliminate its last “premium” first class product, which is the A321T first class cabin, as those planes are replaced by A321XLRs.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that kentucky Rep. James Comer, here talking to reporters on Capitol Hill in June, is running for governor. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    According to recent reports, kentucky Rep. James R. Comer, whose role as chairman of the House Oversight Committee gave him a powerful platform to investigate Democrats, including former Presidents Joe Biden and Bill Clinton, has introduced a run for governor next year.

    According to recent reports, the Republican, who was just elected to a sixth full term representing Kentucky’s 1st District, is seeking to succeed term-limited Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear. Kentucky is one of three states holding off-year gubernatorial elections in 2027, alongside Louisiana and Mississippi.

    In his announcement at a tele-town hall Monday night, Comey emphasized pocketbook problems, pledging to eliminate the state income tax and boost job-creation in Louisville.

    “If we get that income tax to zero, people are going to have more money to spend, and we're going to be able to attract more good-paying jobs to Kentucky, which will be able to keep our best and brightest in the state,’’ he said.

    As the leader of the House Oversight panel, Comer has been at the forefront in the fight over the release of records related to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. (Last week, the committee released a report concluding that the federal government mishandled criminal probes into Epstein’s activities.).

    Comer is a staunch ally of President Donald Trump, who carried Kentucky by 31 points in 2024, and his hard-nosed style of politics is conveyed in a soft-spoken Southern drawl.

    Known back home as Jamie, Comer has deep roots in rural Monroe County, dating back to the late 1700s. Prior to coming to Congress, he operated a farm before serving 11 years in the Kentucky House. In 2011, he was elected as the commonwealth’s commissioner of agriculture.

    It has been revealed that he made an unsuccessful run for governor in 2015, losing the Republican primary by 83 votes to Matt Bevin, who went on to win the general election. The following year, Comer easily won election to the House from his western Kentucky district, succeeding Republican Ed Whitfield.

    Industry observers note that comer has moved quickly to consolidate GOP support for his gubernatorial bid. He already has the backing of Kentucky Sen. Rand Paul and Sen.-elect Andy Barr. Michael Adams, Kentucky’s term-limited secretary of state who’d been seen a potential contender, gave Comer an early endorsement this summer.

    While Comer enters the race as the Republican front-runner, he won’t have the field to himself. Other declared hopefuls include local prosecutor Rick Hardin and distiller Charles “Bruiser” Martin, who appeared on the Discovery Channel show “Moonshiners: Master Distiller.”.

    According to recent reports, while Kentucky has in recent decades grown reliably Republican at the federal level, the GOP has won just two gubernatorial elections there over the past half century. Two high-profile Democrats have already introduced bids to keep the governor’s mansion in party hands: Lt. Gov. Jacqueline Coleman and former state House Majority Leader and Beshear adviser Rocky Adkins, who ran for governor in 2019.

    In a statement Tuesday, the Democratic Governors Association dismissed Comer as “a job-killing, pro-war politician who looks down on everyday Kentuckians.”.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, the first example of the world's first 6th-generation stealth bomber is expected to be 'on the ramp' at Ellsworth Air Force Base sometime in 2027. The US Air Force's B-21 Raider, built by Northrop Grumman, is one of the most resounding successes in recent procurement history for the Department of Defense. Although no official number has been announced for annual production, the Pentagon has already granted a 25% funding increase to expedite initial production.

    The aircraft has been so impressive that the initial fleet size of 100 airframes is already expected to increase, with proponents from the top brass of the Air Force as well as lawmakers on Capitol Hill pushing for 185 or even 200. Based on the publicly available data and these figures, we can estimate that between nine and ten Raiders will likely be built every year, but that could go up to as high as 12 if the total fleet is greatly expanded.

    The assembly line dedicated to the B-21 Raider is at Air Force Plant 42 in Palmdale, California. Northrop Grumman intends to keep the entire operation limited to its historic manufacturing complex at this site, which sprawls over nearly a million square feet, even as the total fleet order grows. Northrop and the USAF have indicated that a larger factory is not needed with digital optimization and shifting some manufacturing burdens to Tier 1 suppliers.

    Recent findings suggest that following the confirmation of a 25% capacity increase at Plant 42, Northrop invested $2.5 billion in capital to modernize the site with automation and other upgrades planned for installation between 2027 and 2029. Kathy Warden, Northrop’s chief executive, was quoted by Air and Space Forces magazine giving these remarks during a discussion at the Bernstein Strategic Decisions Conference in May.

    “As we move through the completion of the test program and into production, we look forward to the opportunity to build these faster—and that’s the agreement that we have now come to with the Air Force—which also opens up the opportunity for [the Air Force] to potentially buy even more...”.

    That increased rate allows [the Air Force] to consider how they meet mission requirements, and how many aircraft they would want to build to do that. They are undertaking that analysis now, and certainly our ability to build faster is a positive factor in those evaluations.”.

    In a recent development, secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth opened the door in April when he told lawmakers that the Air Force will need a lot more than the planned minimum 100 B-21s. Then in May, Lieutenant General David Tabbert testified to Capitol Hill that the service would prepare its revised Raider fleet numbers by Spring 2027.

    Sources indicate that US Navy Admiral Richard Correl, commander of US Strategic Command, testified to Colorado in March that the Air Force would need at least 145 B-21s. He went so far as to propose that opening a second production line may actually be a viable means of achieving that goal. So far, Northrop has not indicated that it has explored this potential yet. Has the organization already spent very large sums out of pocket on Plant 42, that would require another large funding injection.

    Sources indicate that despite the rising investment from the Pentagon, Northrop has spent a considerable amount of its own funds to support the Raider program until federal investment arrives. The company reported a $477 million loss on the first plane after it was delivered in the first quarter of 2025, according to Air and Space Forces magazine. While the B-21 has been an exceptionally smooth development by DOD standards, by leaning on lessons learned from the B-2, it hasn't been without its hiccups.

    The Raider has avoided the notoriety that the B-2 earned when it debuted as the most expensive aircraft ever produced, at about $2 billion per airframe. This time, Northrop has executed an almost flawless program with the B-21. The Spirit is unfairly maligned for that price tag since it only inflated when the fleet size was cut from over 100 to just 20. Warden gave these remarks on the Raider's progression earlier in May.

    “No program is going to be perfect, and so we had that ‘learning,’” Warden noted. “It resulted in some rework, and we took that charge. For a program of this size, complexity, and duration, this program is performing exceptionally well. But any program of this size does carry with it risk, especially as you move into production for the first time.

    But we are retiring those risks with each passing day. As the aircraft tests well, and we get through build processes, we are feeling very positive about our ability to continue to deliver on our estimates.”.

    In November 2026, a B-21 flying from Edwards Air Force Base completed the program’s first weapons release test. The Air Force revealed on November 13 that a conventional munition had been dropped, though it didn’t specify which one, adding that the Raider was moving from a flight test aircraft to a working weapons platform. The test also analyzed thousands of hours of digital twin modeling against a real drop, and it keeps the B-21 on track to reach Ellsworth in 2027.

    The Air Force is working on infrastructure to support B-21s at Ellsworth, Whiteman, and Dyess Air Force Base already in anticipation of transition in the near future. The service is aiming for initial combat readiness in 2027 for the first unit at Ellsworth. Ramping up production now will facilitate faster transition across the follow-on bases in 2029 and beyond. As the total fleet size of Raiders may grow, the number of bases dedicated to the type is likely to follow as well.

    Northrop's chief executive, Warden, expressed confidence that the company could continue building the bombers efficiently while lowering risk as it continues to explore different means to meet higher delivery rates in the future. Building aircraft faster means beddown locations must be ready to receive airframes concurrently rather than sequentially.

    It has been revealed that that is in part already happening with simultaneous overhauls of different scope taking place at each of the three bases already selected. Looking beyond facilities, the formal training unit being stood up at Ellsworth would need to be expanded in order to produce more instructors and graduate more qualified Raider pilots to crew the new stealth bombers as they arrive. All of these efforts would also impact present mission readiness as it would require phasing out of legacy platforms with veteran pilots off the front line to go through the retraining pipeline.

    Sources indicate that the Air Force is working through a complex and lengthy 'divest to invest' fleet modernization strategy that includes retiring the oldest planes while also recapitalizing some vintage warbirds. The best example is the aggressive push to sunset the Fairchild Republic A-10 Warthog while injecting over $20 billion in upgrades for the Boeing B-52 Stratofortress fleet. The B-21 is one of the next-gen platforms that directly benefits when an old Cold War-era plane is sent to the Boneyard.

    Now the A-10 fleet has had its final day extended once again thanks to lawmakers in Washington, but it will inevitably be retired in favor of next-gen aircraft. The old flying tank has been much loved by the troops and aircrew, but Air Force leadership wants to prioritize a latest 'high-low' fleet mix that leverages legacy airframes with performance that complements next-gen platforms. This is why the A-10 gets the ax, but the B-52 gets a makeover.

    At the same time, the B-21 Raider is getting a huge budget boost in order to speed up that fleet recapitalization. As the Stratofortresses go to the depot for overhauls and the Northrop Grumman B-2 Spirits are retired alongside Rockwell B-1 Lancers, a huge capability gap opens up. There is already a readiness level crisis across the Air Force, and at the Air Force Global Strike Command, which is responsible for all three current bomber types.

    Consolidating the fleet into just two types will benefit the Air Force in the long term for cost and readiness factors. In the short term, delivering more B-21s to bomber squadrons allows the Air Force to phase out its legacy platforms that are not being renewed and not only keeping readiness up but greatly increasing it. The AFGSC also gets an exponential combat capability spike every time a new B-21 replaces a B-2 or B-1.

    According to recent reports, another reason that the Air Force wants the B-21s to arrive as soon as possible is to facilitate the transition to a fully compliant agile combat employment fleet. At the moment, the B-2 and the B-1 are far less suited to expeditionary deployments to air bases across the globe than the B-21 will be. In a conflict within the Indo-Pacific, the Air Force can scatter B-21s across smaller allied airfields. This complicates enemy targeting and ensures the fleet cannot be wiped out in a single missile strike at a forward base.

    Notably, the B-52 is better suited to ACE operations than its younger successors as well, thanks to the rugged airframe and simple design. It is not a stealthy plane, but it does offer a massive payload capacity for standoff weapons in both its internal weapons bay and external pylons. This makes it an excellent low-cost supporter, adding magazine depth for B-21s flying in contested airspace where the B-52 can't penetrate.

    Sources indicate that the B-21 is actually smaller than the B-2, which makes the B-52 backup as a 'missile truck' more valuable since it will have a smaller payload. The capacity reduction on the Raider was made consciously for a trade-off in mission capability as it allowed the upcoming sixth-generation bomber to operate freely from virtually any base within the US and allied network around the world. Thus, the USAF is encouraging a rapid spool up in production to replace its restricted B-2 bombers as soon as possible.

    We’ve just seen American formally retire its Boeing 777 first class, and with that, no airline in the United States has a “true” international first class anymore. It’s the end of an era, because going back many decades, premium products were largely pioneered by US carriers. So I think this raises the question — why can US carriers not make first class work in a way that’s economically viable, especially as they keep talking about how premium they are?

    Before we get into this, let me make sure we’re all on the same page when it comes to terms. This post isn’t about the premium cabin on domestic flights, which is often referred to as first class. Instead, it’s about international flights that have a cabin above business class, when it’s marketed as first class. So this would include airlines on my list of the world’s best first class products.

    Airline executives are divided on the merits of having an international first class cabin. Some insist that there’s no need for such a cabin, as business class has improved so much. Meanwhile others absolutely see merit to such a product.

    Industry observers note that I mean, just look at how carriers like Air France, Lufthansa, Singapore Airlines, and SWISS, are all investing in first class. I think Air France’s La Premiere first class is the perfect example of the upside such a product has for an airline:.

    Sources indicate that what’s interesting is that for the airlines that succeed with first class, the single biggest market — and single biggest point of sale — is the United States. So how is it that carriers like Air France, Lufthansa, SWISS, etc., can make money offering first class to the United States (primarily targeting Americans), but US airlines seemingly can’t?

    According to recent reports, the US has way too many people with tens or hundreds of millions of dollars, or even billions of dollars. There are plenty of people who would pay to fly private, and would pay for Air France La Premiere first class, but would never consider paying the high price for first class on a US carrier, because it’s just not worth it.

    When they fly first class, they want this….

    It has been revealed that it’s no surprise that first class at US carriers has historically failed. In many ways, it reflects the failures of the industry from decades past. In other words, first class has long been thought of as “upgrade class,” rather than something actually worth paying for. US carriers have managed to change that narrative on domestic flights, but not so much on international flights.

    What explains the failure of first class at US carriers? If you ask me, here are the main factors:.

    Call it a hot take, but I think international first class absolutely could succeed at a US carrier, if done right, with a couple of caveats. Let me start with the two main hurdles that would need to be overcome, and I’ll acknowledge, this might just be the biggest problem:.

    If those hurdles could be overcome, here’s the play, as I see it (and yes, this is largely inspired by Air France La Premiere):.

    Industry observers note that I think the halo effect of something like this would be massive as well. Seriously, US airline executives love to talk about how premium they are, but they can’t even introduce a top-end product, despite having access to the most lucrative customer base in the world.

    In terms of economics, let me also point out that the opportunity cost of a first class cabin isn’t actually that high. “Premium” is all the rage, so what you do here is eliminate some economy seats:.

    At this point, no airline from the United States offers first class on international flights anymore. For airlines that can’t stop talking about how unbelievably premium they are, I find that to be a pretty perplexing reality. I know that many people have just accepted “oh, a good business class is the future,” but I have a different take.

    It has been revealed that I think no US carrier actually being able to offer a globally competitive product is a failure in strategy and creativity. They have access to the world’s most lucrative customer base, and other airlines can seemingly make money serving US customers with a first class product. The glitch is, US carriers have long not actually given people a reason to fly first class, all while offering too much capacity.

    Personally I think there would be a lot of merit to an international first class product that’s boutique, and is operated in the right markets. That’s not to say that I think it’ll happen — I don’t — but I do think it could succeed. The only real hurdle to overcome would be how to ensure good service….

    Why I’d Pick Economy Over Premium Economy On An Overnight Flight

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1128 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • I just got back to Rio after a quick trip to Ireland for Aer Lingus’ event to showcase their new A330 cabins, including its first-ever premium economy.
    • Sources indicate that I flew Air France economy both ways, and I’m glad I resisted the offer of $420 during online check-in to upgrade the outbound overnight economy leg.
    • In a recent development, however, to answer the economy vs.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    I just got back to Rio after a quick trip to Ireland for Aer Lingus’ event to showcase their new A330 cabins, including its first-ever premium economy.

    Sources indicate that I flew Air France economy both ways, and I’m glad I resisted the offer of $420 during online check-in to upgrade the outbound overnight economy leg. Ironically, it was the long day-flight back where I actually wished I’d upgraded.

    In a recent development, however, to answer the economy vs. premium economy question, it all comes down to maximising comfort, and I think this is easier to do in economy than premium economy.

    If, like me, sleeping upright or on your back is almost impossible, then what follows will likely apply to you.

    The main reason I’m deterred to pick premium economy for overnight flights is because of the fixed armrests, where tray tables are sometimes stowed in this cabin.

    Despite the extra recline and leg rest element (which sometimes makes it even harder to get comfortable), the fixed armrests restrict the ability to sleep any way other than straight like a pencil.

    To make matters worse, they stop you from lying across more than one seat if you find yourself in an empty row.

    It’s for that reason that I much prefer economy. While having a row to yourself isn’t guaranteed, there’s at least a chance of being able to move around the cabin, or stretch out into an empty seat. No matter where you sit or how empty the cabin is, you can’t do that in premium economy.

    Another element of my pre-trip planning that I expect many of you to relate to is the fact it takes me so long umming and aahing over the best seat to pick.

    Thanks to my Flying Blue Gold status (SkyTeam Elite Plus), I could pick any seat in the economy cabin of the Boeing 777-200ER for free from 72 hours before departure.

    I narrowed it down to an empty seat in the exit row, and the only row of three with an empty middle seat. I didn’t even consider one of the many empty middle rows of four seats in case they filled up before take off and I ended up in an aisle with no window to rest my head. Using the window or plane’s fuselage to rest my head on is the only saving grace for me when trying to sleep sitting upright.

    As the empty exit seat would have the same restricting fixed partition as premium, I decided against that, too.

    According to recent reports, after the “boarding complete” announcement was made, the middle seat in my row remained empty, and there were three seats free in the middle of row 25, a row in front. I explained to the girl in the aisle seat that if one of us moved to the other row, we’d both have three seats to ourselves. She didn’t seem to understand my point, and noted she’d prefer to sit in the aisle than us both have three free seats to ourselves.

    I didn’t want to move to the middle seats either, so I got as comfortable as I could using the middle seat and the pillow I brought from home.

    Industry observers note that in the end, I did manage to get some half decent curled up shut eye (the thick pillow protected my back from the hard parts of the seat when propped against the fuselage). However, when I went to the loo, I noticed some people in the rear cabin had got lucky and were fast asleep spread across a whole four seats.

    Maybe I’ll take more of a risk next time….

    Sources indicate that I’m not saying economy is always a better choice than premium. For example, I’d always recommend Emirates’ pretty darn impressive premium economy over economy, because it genuinely is several steps up from economy.

    According to recent reports, if it was up to me, I’d have had a lie-flat seat for the overnight segment. I didn’t, and I’m pretty certain I got better sleep quality curled up across two seats in economy that I would have almost upright on my back in premium.

    Would you ever choose economy over premium economy?

    Premium Upgrade? United Airlines Is Replacing Its Remaining Boeing 767s With 787 Dreamliners

    📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1513 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • On September 8, 1982, United Airlines brought the Boeing 767 into commercial service, revolutionizing its long-haul network with a twin-engine aircraft that could safely operate transatlantic routes dominated by quadjets.
    • It has been revealed that united has historically relied on the 767 to serve European cities 'across the pond.' Now, United intends to retire all of these aircraft by 2030.
    • The post-pandemic rise in demand for year-round leisure and business travel to Europe reshaped United's business model around a 'premiumized' cabin.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    On September 8, 1982, United Airlines brought the Boeing 767 into commercial service, revolutionizing its long-haul network with a twin-engine aircraft that could safely operate transatlantic routes dominated by quadjets. The airline still uses 53 of these legacy twinjets to anchor its transatlantic network from Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR) and Washington Dulles International Airport (IAD) more than 40 years later. The current fleet consists of 16 stretched 767-400ER aircraft with an average age of 23 years and 37 older 767-300ER aircraft with an average age of 29.

    It has been revealed that united has historically relied on the 767 to serve European cities 'across the pond.' Now, United intends to retire all of these aircraft by 2030. To attract surging transatlantic travel demand without flooding routes with low-margin coach tickets, United is deploying 222-seat Elevated Boeing 787-9s featuring 99 premium seats, including 64 enclosed Polaris suites and 35 Premium Plus recliners, alongside stretched 787-10s for slot-constrained hubs like London Heathrow Airport (LHR).

    The post-pandemic rise in demand for year-round leisure and business travel to Europe reshaped United's business model around a 'premiumized' cabin. The Dreamliner's wider composite fuselage accommodates spacious suites in the front of the cabin with a lower 6,000-foot (1,829-meter) cabin altitude and higher air humidity, which softens jet lag regardless of seat number. Combined with 25% better fuel efficiency over the 767, these upgrades let United expand premium capacity and passenger comfort on top European routes and lower operating costs.

    According to recent reports, moving from the 1980s-era 767 to the 787 Dreamliner improves passenger appeal but also route flexibility. While the 767's flight range is limited to roughly 5,980 nautical miles (11,075 km), the next-gen 787-9 flies up to 7,565 nautical miles (14,010 km). Its faster Mach 0.85 cruise speed also shaves up to 50 minutes off eastbound Atlantic crossings, helping United meet tight European airport arrival slots while easily rotating aircraft onto Pacific routes on the West Coast for seasonal destinations.

    According to recent reports, in 2022, following a landmark order for 100 787s and an option to buy 100 more, United CEO Scott Kirby gave these remarks: "United emerged from the pandemic as the world's leading global airline and the flag carrier of the US. This order further solidifies our lead and creates new opportunities ... to connect more people to more places around the globe and deliver the best experience in the sky.".

    Stan Deal, president and CEO of Boeing Commercial Airplanes, also offered this comment: "With this investment in its future fleet, the 737. The Boeing team is honored by United's trust in our family of airplanes to connect people and transport cargo around the world for decades to come.".

    Evolving from aluminum to composite jets not only makes the passenger experience better but also opens up more freight revenue for UA. The 767-300ER maxes out at 412,000 pounds (186,880 kg). In comparison, United can transport up to 52,400 pounds (23,768 kg) of high-margin commercial freight in the belly on each transatlantic flight, with the 787-9's increased maximum takeoff weight of 560,000 pounds (254,011 kg). That's before all the other improvements the Dreamliner delivers.

    In a recent development, passengers traveling across the Atlantic will see immediate changes on the flightline and inside the cabin when the outdated 767s are retired in favor of 787 Dreamliners. The wider composite cabin significantly improves personal living space across all seating classes as compared to the tiny 1980s-era 767 configuration. While older 767s had open, doorless business seats and tight overhead bins, the forthcoming Elevated 787-9s feature enclosed Polaris suites with sliding privacy doors, wireless charging, and larger 4K TVs.

    Industry observers note that economy class passengers also benefit from wider aisles, sculpted sidewalls, dynamic LED mood lighting to facilitate time-zone transitions, and oversized overhead bins that can carry each passenger's roll-aboard bags. Additionally, the 787's single-piece carbon-fiber body can withstand substantially higher internal pressure without experiencing metal fatigue, enabling the cabin to maintain a comfortable 6,000 feet (1,829 meters) of pressure with 16% air humidity.

    Meanwhile, the 767 must maintain cabin pressure at the old standard of 8,000 feet (2,438 meters) in simulated elevation. It must also maintain air humidity below 10% to prevent metal joints from rusting, since a conventional riveted aluminum fuselage bends and stresses under high air pressure. After seven hours in the air overnight, passengers benefit from the increased blood oxygen level that the 787 delivers.

    Sources indicate that that means fewer headaches and substantially reduced jet lag thanks to the lower cabin altitude and additional moisture. Dreamliner windows are also 65% larger than those on the 767 and use electronic dimming controls rather than plastic pull blinds to manage sunlight. The Dreamliner cabin is also significantly quieter during takeoff and cruise thanks to sophisticated acoustic insulation surrounding the engine nacelles and the lack of noisy high-pressure air lines for sub-systems because of its all-electric architecture.

    Despite UA's rapid trajectory of 'premiumization,' Boeing must resolve significant assembly delays at its North Charleston facility in order to support the airline's goals. In order to replace its 53 outdated 767s, United Airlines updated its backlog to a firm order for 150 Boeing 787 Dreamliners, with options for a further 50. However, production was delayed considerably by Federal Aviation Administration safety inspections following quality problems with composite materials. Due to these delays, United was obliged to reduce the number of Boeing aircraft it planned to deliver in the near future from 165 to just 63, delaying the majority of latest widebody deliveries until after 2026.

    In a recent development, in 2023, Kirby gave this enhancement on the UA fleet: "Our planning and focus on the long term have helped us surge past other airlines that stood still. I'm convinced our strategy is the right one as we continue to add new, larger aircraft to take full advantage of our growing flying opportunities both internationally and domestically.".

    In a recent development, meanwhile, Deal spoke for Boeing and added these remarks: "United's unprecedented commitment to the 787 Dreamliner family is a testament to the market-leading operating economics and reliability of Boeing's widebody jets. With the 787, United will enjoy all the synergies of operating one of the largest, most efficient fleets in the skies.".

    Industry observers note that united will still be forced to spend millions of dollars maintaining the safe operation of 30-year-old aluminum aircraft while waiting years for delayed Dreamliners. High-time 767-300ER and 767-400ER aircraft are subjected to extensive, costly structural inspections by mechanics rather than being retired to desert storage. In order to make up for the timetable deficit, older aircraft, such as tail N641UA, which has nearly 100,000 flight hours and 20,000 landings, require expensive overhauls on their older General Electric engines in addition to thorough wing and tail scanning inspections.

    Recent findings suggest that after taking a $200 million financial hit from factory delays and plane groundings, United CEO Scott Kirby put together a backup strategy. Along with leasing 35 Airbus A321neo jets to cover short-term domestic flights, Kirby kept United's delayed order for 45 Airbus A350-900 widebodies alive. Holding onto those European factory slots gives United a real alternative if Boeing's South Carolina assembly delays continue.

    Industry observers note that moving from the Boeing 767-300ER to the 787-9 represents a major leap forward in jet engine design, which enables greater range and payload as well as better fuel burn rates. United's older 767s run on Pratt & Whitney PW4060 or General Electric CF6-80C2B6F engines built with 94-inch (239 cm) titanium fans and a 4.8:1 bypass ratio, producing around 60,200 pounds of thrust (268 kN). In contrast, the 787-9 uses General Electric GEnx-1B engines rated up to 75,000 pounds of thrust (334 kN).

    The GEnx features 111-inch (282 cm) carbon-fiber fan blades, a lightweight composite fan case that cuts over 400 pounds (181 kg) per engine, and an 8.8:1 bypass ratio that trims fuel burn by over 20% while cutting nitrogen oxide emissions by 55%. Additionally, the two generations also differ in how each aircraft powers its internal systems.

    Industry observers note that in order to run the cabin air conditioning, start the engines, and heat the wings against ice, the 767 uses a conventional bleed-air configuration that draws hot compressed air above 392°F (200°C) straight from the engine cores, depriving the turbines of useful power. In order to improve engine efficiency and reduce cruise fuel consumption by about 4%, Boeing replaced the titanium air ducts on the 787 with an all-electric system powered by four engine-mounted generators that produce 1.4 megawatts of electricity.

    Since the 767's body is made of conventional aluminum sheets welded over metal ribs, it is susceptible to rust and metal fatigue during thousands of pressurization cycles. In contrast, the 787 uses single-piece body sections and long, thin wings that flex upward by roughly 10 feet (3 meters) at the tips during flight to smooth out turbulence and reduce air drag at Mach 0.85. Strong carbon-fiber composites constitute half of the 787's structural weight.

    What Republicans don’t know about Black voters’ resilience cost them

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1010 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that sen.-elect Scott Colom speaks during a victory rally at Tougaloo College on Nov.
    • The campaign of Mississippi’s Sen.-elect Scott Colom was rightfully praised for its clever and brutal ads.
    • According to recent reports, however, it was fitting that the Democrat’s closing message traded the edge for a solemn reminder of who and what brought him so far on his journey to his election as Mississippi’s first Black U.S.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that sen.-elect Scott Colom speaks during a victory rally at Tougaloo College on Nov. 11. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images).

    The campaign of Mississippi’s Sen.-elect Scott Colom was rightfully praised for its clever and brutal ads. The “pick another protein” spot will forever be stuck in the brains of a huge swath of Americans, especially Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith. She underestimated Colom and his team, and will soon be an ex-senator.

    According to recent reports, however, it was fitting that the Democrat’s closing message traded the edge for a solemn reminder of who and what brought him so far on his journey to his election as Mississippi’s first Black U.S. senator since Reconstruction.

    The ad delivered an all-American lesson about history, born of bravery and sacrifice.

    Filmed at the Jackson, Miss., home of slain civil rights leader Medgar Evers, the ad featured Colom recounting the story of Evers, a World War II veteran who survived Normandy, only to be shot in the back by a racist assassin, resentful that a Black man dared to exercise his rights as a citizen in the country he fought for.

    Sources indicate that “He was killed for helping Mississippians vote,” Colom said. “On Tuesday, use your vote and honor everyone who died for that right.”.

    In a state where voting is still racially polarized, it was clear that Colom would not win over a majority of white voters; he won an estimated 25 percent, better than Democrats in recent elections and cutting into Trump’s margins, but certainly not a path to victory.

    Black voters in Mississippi made the difference, as they often have. With their allies in the cause of justice, they heeded the call. They revealed up despite the state’s stringent and often confusing voting restrictions, purges of the voting rolls engineered by Republican Secretary of State Michael Watson (who used unverified data from a credit bureau), and the U.S. Supreme Court Louisiana v. Callais decision that led to a wave of Southern states breaking up Black-majority districts.

    When the Mississippi purges resulted in “affidavit ballots” that required verification to count, as The Washington Post reported, young Black women tracked down those voters, one by one, to do everything they could to ensure voters’ efforts were not in vain.

    Black voters mattered in states all over the country, but especially in the South, where low turnout has plagued Democrats, particularly in midterm elections.

    Keisha Lance Bottoms was elected the first Black female governor in the country in Georgia, where Democrats won up and down the ballot. Newly elected senators Annie Andrews in South Carolina and James Talarico of Texas campaigned for and earned support from Black voters with proposals that rose above platitudes. And don’t sleep on North Carolina, where voters flipped seats the GOP tried to gerrymander into a hardened majority. The sight of hundreds of students from HBCU NC A&T State University, denied a campus early voting site, marching to the polls, must have made the ancestors smile.

    In Florida and Louisiana, where Democrats had little financial support and lost their statewide races, Black voters brought them tantalizingly close to victory and energized for the contests to come.

    I still don’t expect Republicans to give up the election shenanigans, done in the name of “election integrity” and color blindness but in reality designed to demoralize as much as suppress. Why try to win over a diverse electorate with an inclusive, policy-driven message when manipulating Black-majority districts can still work?

    Recent findings suggest that the number of Black U.S. House members in the next session of Congress will fall, offset by a few Democrats who survived in redrawn districts, including Shomari Figures of Alabama and Don Davis of North Carolina.

    But you can’t redistrict a state, and you can’t skip town halls and expect tradition, support for the Confederacy and an “R” after your name to forever save you — the Hyde-Smith playbook.

    "I blocked Scott Colom from being a federal judge, and you blocked him from being U.S. senator," she bragged, too soon, on election night.

    Maybe she should have emphasized affordability, saving rural hospitals and serving all Mississippians, as Colom did.

    What did GOP officials in those Southern red states think they would accomplish by focusing on their base and ignoring everyone else in states they were supposed to be serving?

    Did they not pay attention in history class, or maybe they attended one of those post-integration private schools where an unedited version of America’s past might not have been on the lesson strategy?

    Did they believe that voters who remembered Evers, Fannie Lou Hamer, Vernon Dahmer and countless others would shrug and say “you win” when legislatures and elections officials quickly and cynically pounced to quiet their voices?

    That would be disrespectful to all the people who worked for, sometimes died for rights they knew they may never enjoy, yet had a belief in America and the rightness of their cause.

    In a recent development, scott Colom and the Evers family remembered. He was emotional in his reaction, in an MS NOW interview, when asked about the statement from Reena Evers-Everette, daughter of Medgar and Myrlie Evers. “Their courage helped make this moment possible,” she stated.

    Colum agreed: “I absolutely stand on their shoulders. And from the bottom of my heart, I’m going to do everything I can to make them proud.”.

    Post-election, he has been very gracious, saying that he intends to serve all Mississippians, including the woman whom I suspect would hit a different note if the election had turned in her favor.

    In a recent development, I have no doubt Scott Colom means it. He knows who paid the price to get him this far.

    Tech Report: Third Time’s Not The Charm: A SWISS A220’s Odd Triple Aborted Takeoff

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (975 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • If you’re a frequent flyer, odds are that you’ve encountered an aborted takeoff, whereby the plane accelerates down the runway, only to slow down, and eventually come to a stop.
    • However, here’s something you don’t often see — a SWISS Airbus A220 aborted its takeoff three times in a row, before finally returning to the gate to see what was going on, as reported by Blick.
    • In a recent development, on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, SWISS flight LX2110 was scheduled to operate from Zurich (ZRH) to Malaga (AGP), with a 9:35AM departure.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    If you’re a frequent flyer, odds are that you’ve encountered an aborted takeoff, whereby the plane accelerates down the runway, only to slow down, and eventually come to a stop. In some cases this can feel like a non-event, while in other cases it can feel much scarier, depending on the speed at which the takeoff is aborted.

    However, here’s something you don’t often see — a SWISS Airbus A220 aborted its takeoff three times in a row, before finally returning to the gate to see what was going on, as reported by Blick. The explanation is actually quite logical, but that doesn’t make the whole ordeal any less unusual.

    In a recent development, on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, SWISS flight LX2110 was scheduled to operate from Zurich (ZRH) to Malaga (AGP), with a 9:35AM departure. The flight was operated by an Airbus A220-300 with the registration code HB-JCM.

    The plane pushed back and taxied out to the runway right on schedule. The pilots began the takeoff roll, but then promptly applied the brakes, causing the plane to come to a stop, while still at a slow speed. The pilots took a moment to run checklists, and then decided on another takeoff attempt, only for the same thing to happen again!

    It has been revealed that after the second aborted takeoff, the captain reportedly informed passengers that the thrust levers had popped out during the takeoff roll, and that was the reason for the aborted takeoff. However, rather than returning to the gate, they decided to attempt an additional takeoff roll.

    Once again, the takeoff was aborted. At that point the captain explained that nothing like this had ever happened to him before in his 12 year career, and that the plane would be returning to the gate.

    There ended up being a plane change, and then the A220 with the registration code HB-JCO was assigned to operate this flight — it ended up taking off at 1:29PM and landing at 3:52PM, around 3.5 hours behind schedule.

    A SWISS spokesperson confirmed the incident happened, though noted that the takeoffs were aborted at a low speed of around 50 kilometers per hour (around 30 miles per hour).

    What explains the aborted takeoffs? Well, it was because as the plane accelerated for takeoff, the automatic thrust control system automatically deactivated. To explain this as simply as possible, as I understand it, on the A220 when the auto-thrust is armed and the thrust levers are moved forward for takeoff, the auto-thrust then takes over, and moves the levers forward without manual intervention.

    In a recent development, in other words, one of the pilots keeps their hands on the auto-thrust levers and “moves” with them, but doesn’t actually apply any force. Pilots are trained this way, and to not manually apply force. In the event that the crew tries to stop the auto-thrust lever motion, a pressure switch detects this, and then disengages the auto-thrust, to allow for a manual override.

    In this case, the auto-thrust incorrectly detected resistance, when the pilots weren’t attempting to apply it. According to the airline, the system that monitors the aircraft’s technical status in real time was unable to identify the cause of the error, as no errors were displayed in the system. So at first, the pilots likely wondered if they had accidentally applied force.

    However, once technicians had a look at the plane, it was discovered that the switch for disabling the automatic thrust control on the original aircraft was stuck, and this caused the automatic thrust control to shut down during takeoff attempts.

    Industry observers note that so while this can understandably seem scary to passengers, this wasn’t even a direct safety glitch. After all, the pilots could’ve also manually moved the throttles. However, you also don’t want to take off when you know there’s an issue with the throttles, since that’s not exactly a best practice.

    According to recent reports, A SWISS Airbus A220 attempted a takeoff from Zurich three times in a row. While I’ve had two consecutive aborted takeoffs, I’ve never had three, and I can’t imagine that happens all too often.

    According to recent reports, while this is unusual, it sounds like this was handled well, and I can see why the pilots kept trying. This wasn’t a critical safety issue, but instead, just an incorrect detection of inputs, in a way that wouldn’t really pose a risk to the flight. At the same time, you don’t want to knowingly take off with a fault switch.

    What do you make of this SWISS aborted takeoff trio?
