    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • American Express is best known for its points-earning cards, but the Blue Cash Everyday® Card from American Express proves that Amex can do cash back well too.
    • According to recent reports, if you’re looking for a simple card that earns a solid return at supermarkets, gas stations, and online retailers, this one is worth a look.
    • This post is my in-depth Blue Cash Everyday Card review, so I’ll cover the bonus categories, the credits and perks, and how this card compares to both the Blue Cash Preferred® Card from American Express and the Citi Double Cash® Card.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    American Express is best known for its points-earning cards, but the Blue Cash Everyday® Card from American Express proves that Amex can do cash back well too.

    According to recent reports, if you’re looking for a simple card that earns a solid return at supermarkets, gas stations, and online retailers, this one is worth a look. It has no annual fee (Rates & Fees), a decent welcome bonus, a great intro APR offer, and some useful bonus categories that cover a good chunk of everyday spending.

    This post is my in-depth Blue Cash Everyday Card review, so I’ll cover the bonus categories, the credits and perks, and how this card compares to both the Blue Cash Preferred® Card from American Express and the Citi Double Cash® Card.

    Review: Learn more about the Blue Cash Everyday® Card from American Express.

    First, here’s an overview of the Amex Blue Cash Everyday benefits and value proposition, from fees, to rewards, to the welcome bonus:.

    I also put together my list of pros and cons for the Blue Cash Everyday Card:.

    When applying for a credit card, obviously the welcome offer, eligibility rules, and fees, are major considerations. So below I’ll cover the details of that for the Amex Blue Cash Everyday.

    Sources indicate that the Amex Blue Cash Everyday is offering the following welcome bonus: You may be eligible for as high as $200 cash back after spending $2,000 in purchases on your fresh Card in the first 6 months. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer. Cash back is received as Reward Dollars, redeemable for statement credit or for other select options. Terms Apply.

    That’s a reasonable bonus for a no annual fee card, and the spending requirement is low enough that most people should be able to hit it. However, it’s also not that much to get excited about, compared to some of the other welcome offers out there.

    Amex cards tend to be fairly easy to get approved for if you have excellent credit. Here are the main rules to be aware of:.

    In a recent development, amex also has a pre-application eligibility tool that lets you check whether you’ll be approved for the card without any impact on your credit score. This is worth using if you’re not sure that you’ll qualify.

    Sources indicate that the Blue Cash Everyday Card has no annual fee. Not the first year, not ever. That alone makes it worth considering as a long-term card in your wallet, even if it’s not your primary spender.

    Holding no annual fee cards long term is also a great way to help your credit score. About 30% of your score comes from credit utilization (the more available credit you have but don’t use, the better), and 15% comes from credit history length (the older your average account age, the better). A no annual fee card you keep open for years helps on both fronts.

    The Blue Cash Everyday Card does have foreign transaction fees (2.7%) (Rates & Fees), so I wouldn’t use it for purchases in foreign currencies. Stick to domestic spending with this one, and find a card with no foreign transaction fees if you’ll be spending time abroad.

    The Amex Blue Cash Everyday has three main bonus categories, each earning 3% cash back on up to $6,000 per year in purchases (then 1%).

    Recent findings suggest that with the Blue Cash Everyday, you earn 3% back at U.S. supermarkets on up to $6,000 per year (then 1%). Earning 3% back at supermarkets with no annual fee is a solid deal, and this is one of the better no annual fee cards for U.S. supermarket spending.

    As with most grocery bonus categories, this generally won’t include warehouse clubs (like Costco), superstores (like Walmart or Target), convenience stores, or discount stores. Traditional supermarkets and grocery chains are what you’re looking for.

    With the Blue Cash Everyday, you also earn 3% back at U.S. gas stations on up to $6,000 per year (then 1%). This is one of the better no annual fee cards for gas station spending.

    It has been revealed that this is the bonus category that makes the Blue Cash Everyday stand out from its siblings. You earn 3% back on U.S. online retail purchases on up to $6,000 per year (then 1%). This covers purchases made on a website or app from a U.S. retail merchant that sells physical goods directly to consumers.

    Industry observers note that given how much shopping happens online these days, this can be a really valuable category. You won’t find this bonus on many other cards.

    Industry observers note that for purchases outside the bonus categories, you earn 1% cash back. This is where the card falls short. At just 1% on non-bonused spending, you’ll definitely want to pair this with a card that offers a better return on everyday purchases.

    With the Amex Blue Cash Everyday, you earn Reward Dollars that can be redeemed as statement credits at a rate of 1.0 cents per point, and there’s no minimum cash back balance required before you can redeem.

    It’s simple and straightforward, though it’s worth knowing that you can’t use cash back to pay your minimum payment due.

    Benefits and credits can certainly help with justifying holding onto credit cards. In the case of the Amex Blue Cash Everyday, you wouldn’t expect very valuable perks, given the card’s lack of an annual fee. However, it’s an area where I’d say the card actually exceeds expectations, and offers solid value.

    Sources indicate that the Blue Cash Everyday offers up to $7 back per month (up to $84 per year) as a statement credit when you use your enrolled Blue Cash Everyday to purchase a subscription, including a bundle subscription, on DisneyPlus.com, Hulu.com, or Stream.ESPN.com U.S. websites, with no minimum purchase requirement. Subscriptions are subject to auto-renewal. If you already pay for any of those services, this is an easy credit to use. (Enrollment required).

    It has been revealed that you can also earn up to $15 per month (up to $180 per year) in statement credits when you purchase Home Chef meal solutions online with your Blue Cash Everyday Card. If you use Home Chef, this is a significant benefit. If you don’t, it’s probably not worth signing up just for the credit. (Enrollment required).

    According to recent reports, the Blue Cash Everyday Card also offers 0% intro APR on purchases and balance transfers for 15 months from the date of account opening. After that, the variable APR is at the moment between 19.74% - 28.74% (Rates & Fees).

    According to recent reports, I generally recommend avoiding financing purchases through credit cards. But if a short-term 0% APR opportunity can help you manage a large purchase and you can pay it off before the rate increases, it’s a nice option to have.

    Another card benefit is access to Amex Presale Tickets® and Amex Reserved Tickets®, which can come in handy if you’re trying to score tickets to an in-demand concert or sporting event.

    Sources indicate that every Amex card gives you access to the Amex Offers program, which provides targeted deals with a variety of retailers. Different cards get different offers, so having multiple Amex cards means more chances to save.

    In a recent development, I try to have as many Amex cards as possible specifically to take advantage of this. Having a no annual fee card like this is ideal, since the card isn’t costing you anything, but you’re still getting access to potentially valuable offers.

    In a recent development, the Amex Blue Cash Everyday comes with coverage to protect your rental car when you charge the rental to this card. The coverage applies for eligible damage or theft, and it’s secondary, so it kicks in after your own car insurance. There are some exclusions, and it doesn’t include liability coverage, so check your card benefits guide for the full details.

    Car rental loss and damage insurance: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Manufacturer. Car Rental Loss or Damage Coverage is offered through American Express Travel Related Services Company, Inc.

    Sources indicate that the Blue Cash Everyday Card also offers purchase protection of up to $1,000 per covered purchase for up to 90 days from the purchase date. You need to pay with the card in order to take advantage of this coverage.

    According to recent reports, the Amex Blue Cash Everyday Card is a solid no annual fee cash back card with useful bonus categories at supermarkets, gas stations, and online retailers. The 3% rate in those categories is strong for a no annual fee card, and the Disney streaming credits, Home Chef credits, and Amex Offers add extra value on top.

    While there are several reasons to consider the Blue Cash Everyday Card, there are also a couple of alternatives that I think are better for most people.

    If you generally like the idea of the Blue Cash Everyday Card, there might still be a better play here. The Blue Cash Preferred® Card from American Express (learn more) is the premium version of the card, and it could be worth applying for it instead (Enrollment is required for select benefits).

    The massive question is whether the Preferred’s $0 intro annual fee for the first year, then $95. annual fee (Rates & Fees) is worth the upgrade. If you spend at least $267 per month at U.S. supermarkets, the extra 3% (the Preferred earns 6% cash back at U.S. supermarkets on up to $6,000 per year in purchases, then 1%) on groceries alone will cover the fee. The Preferred also adds 6% cash back on select U.S. streaming and 3% on transit, which the Everyday doesn’t offer.

    Sources indicate that on the flip side, the Everyday has two things the Preferred doesn’t: 3% on U.S. online retail purchases and a 0% intro APR offer. If you do a lot of online shopping and not as much grocery shopping, the Everyday could be the better card.

    In a recent development, one nice thing is that you could start with the Blue Cash Preferred (with a $0 intro annual fee for the first year, then $95.), and if the math doesn’t work out, downgrade to the Blue Cash Everyday after year one. That way you get the bigger welcome bonus and can test the higher earning rates.

    While there are lots to like about the Blue Cash Everyday, it’s also not particularly well-rounded if you’re looking for an all-in-one cash back credit card.

    Sources indicate that the card offers 3% cash back at U.S. supermarkets, U.S. gas stations, and U.S. online retail purchases (up to certain limits), but on other purchases you’ll earn 1% cash back.

    Sources indicate that everyone will have to crunch the numbers for themselves, but 1% cash back is pretty uncompetitive nowadays for savvy consumers. For example, the no annual fee Citi Double Cash® Card (learn more) offers 1% cash back when you make a purchase, and 1% cash back when you pay for that purchase (in the form of ThankYou points).

    Industry observers note that the Blue Cash Everyday wins in its bonus categories, earning 3% at supermarkets, gas stations, and online retailers compared to the Double Cash’s flat 2%. But the Double Cash wins everywhere else, earning 2% on all purchases versus just 1%.

    If your spending is heavily concentrated in supermarkets, gas, and online shopping, the Blue Cash Everyday will earn you more. If your spending is more spread out across lots of different categories, the Double Cash’s flat 2% on everything will likely come out ahead.

    The Double Cash also has a major advantage in flexibility. Its ThankYou points can be transferred to airline and hotel partners (in conjunction with a premium Citi card like the Citi Strata Premier® Card), giving those points the potential to be worth well more than 2 cents each. The Blue Cash Everyday’s rewards are purely cash back.

    Recent findings suggest that the ideal setup? Have both. Use the Blue Cash Everyday for supermarkets, gas, and online retail where it earns 3%, and the Double Cash for everything else at 2%.

    In a recent development, I think the Blue Cash Everyday is a very decent cash back card with bonus categories most spenders can take advantage of. The card’s main weakness is the 1% rate on everything outside the bonus categories — and even on those categories once you reach the annual cap. For that reason, I’d recommend pairing it with a flat-rate card like the Citi Double Cash (2% on everything) to fill in the gaps. Together, they make a simple, effective, no annual fee credit card cash back setup.

    In a recent development, if you find yourself spending more at supermarkets over time, you can always upgrade to the Blue Cash Preferred for that 6% supermarket rate. But for a no annual fee, low-maintenance starting point, the Blue Cash Everyday is a great choice.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The may be the entry-level card option for Atmos Rewards, but it's anything but basic. This card packs a punch with a free checked bag and preferred boarding on Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines flights, with a fan-favorite $99 Companion Fare for cardholders who meet the spending requirements.

    It has been revealed that even if you don't fly Alaska or Hawaiian often, the points you earn on the card can help you get outsized value. With a robust network of Oneworld and nonalliance partners, Atmos Rewards can take you just about anywhere in the world. Card rating*: ⭐⭐⭐⭐.

    *Card rating is based on the opinion of TPG's editors and is not influenced by the card issuer.

    The is a cobranded airline card within Atmos Rewards, the joint loyalty program between Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines.

    For a $95 annual fee, the card earns valuable Atmos Rewards points and provides a few added benefits.

    Some of the best ways to maximize these points include redeeming for premium cabins with Oneworld partners, such as Cathay Pacific and Fiji Airways. However, Atmos Rewards points are also solid for short-haul domestic routes on Alaska Airlines and American Airlines.

    One of the card's standout perks is its annual $99 Companion Fare (plus taxes and fees from $23) that is earned each account anniversary as long as you've spent $6,000 or more in the prior anniversary year.

    Generally, it's a solid option for Alaska Airlines or Hawaiian Airlines frequent flyers, thanks to the perks provided when flying with either airline, such as free checked bags and preferred boarding.

    However, if you're looking for more premium perks like lounge access, this card won't meet your needs.

    Related: Which credit card should you use for Alaska Airlines flights?

    It has been revealed that the offers fewer benefits than other cobranded airline cards. However, you can still expect some perks.

    According to recent reports, cardholders receive one piece of free checked luggage for themselves and up to six other passengers on the same reservation when flying Alaska or Hawaiian and paying with the Atmos Rewards Ascent. That can save $45 per person each way on most itineraries, though the first checked bag still costs $30 on intra-Hawaii flights.

    Cardholders also get preferred boarding on Alaska and Hawaiian, and they'll receive 20% back on inflight purchases with both airlines when they use the card.

    If you're working toward Atmos Rewards status, you can earn 1 status point for every $3 spent on the card, with no cap on the number of status points you can earn through spending.

    Sources indicate that as mentioned above, one of the best benefits of the Atmos Rewards Ascent is the $99 Companion Fare (plus taxes and fees from $23). This can be unlocked after spending $6,000 or more on the card within the prior anniversary year.

    You'll get value from this perk as long as you fly Alaska Airlines or Hawaiian Airlines with a friend or family member on paid fares at least once a year.

    It has been revealed that carly Helfand, TPG's director of content strategy, previously used the Ascent's Companion Fare to take a last-minute trip to Chicago with her husband. The round-trip flights from Portland International Airport (PDX) in Oregon to Chicago's O'Hare International Airport (ORD) cost $542.60 per person, but she paid $679.63 for both tickets thanks to the Companion Fare.

    It has been revealed that while the Atmos Rewards Ascent doesn't provide outright lounge access, you can get $100 off an annual Alaska Lounge+ membership when you pay with this card. A membership costs $795 per year.

    This benefit alone offsets the card's $95 annual fee. However, given how expensive membership is, this perk isn't too useful unless you were already going to pay for an Alaska Lounge+ membership.

    Recent findings suggest that americans should expect their federal agencies to be staffed by experts who gather evidence meticulously before proposing regulations disinterestedly. But that’s not what the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) has done when it comes to personalized pricing.

    Last month, the FTC ordered nine major companies — Delta Air Lines, Uber, and Instacart among them — “to provide detailed information that will allow the agency to study the use of personal data to set prices and compensation.” The agency, however, seems to have reached its conclusions already, given the contents of both its order and an enforcement policy proposed in August, which appears partial against personalized pricing and the businesses that employ it.

    Vladlena Klymova is a policy analyst at the Taxpayers Protection Alliance.

    #65481. Industry News: Boeing's New Air Force One Still Hasn't Flown & Here's Why

    📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1663 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Boeing's New Air Force One Still Hasn't Flown & Here's Why

    📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1663 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that the Boeing 747 may have ended its commercial production run, but two of the most consequential examples ever built remain deep inside a modification program that has stretched years beyond its original timetable.
    • It has been revealed that that means the aircraft popularly described as the “new Air Force One” remain unfinished even as another Boeing 747-8 has temporarily taken over some presidential duties.
    • Recent findings suggest that the scale of the delay becomes clearer when compared with the original schedule.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that the Boeing 747 may have ended its commercial production run, but two of the most consequential examples ever built remain deep inside a modification program that has stretched years beyond its original timetable. Boeing’s two purpose-built VC-25B presidential aircraft, which are the long-awaited replacements for the US Air Force’s aging VC-25As, were originally expected to be delivered by the end of 2024. Instead, the first aircraft is now scheduled for roughly mid-2028, while the second is expected around mid-2029.

    It has been revealed that that means the aircraft popularly described as the “new Air Force One” remain unfinished even as another Boeing 747-8 has temporarily taken over some presidential duties. This separate, former Qatari 747-8 “Bridge” aircraft carried President Donald Trump for the first time on July 1, according to Air & Space Forces Magazine. The distinction is important: the Bridge jet is an interim solution, while Boeing’s two permanent VC-25Bs remain an extraordinarily complicated engineering project involving secure communications, defensive systems, specialized interiors, structural changes, thousands of wiring modifications, and requirements unlike those of virtually any other passenger aircraft.

    Recent findings suggest that the scale of the delay becomes clearer when compared with the original schedule. Boeing signed the deal in 2018 to convert two Boeing 747-8 Intercontinental airframes into the next generation of presidential transports, with the aircraft originally targeted for completion by the end of 2024. Air & Space Forces Magazine reported in December 2025 that the Air Force was instead projecting the first aircraft for mid-2028 to 2029 after a series of earlier schedule revisions.

    The two aircraft themselves have an unusual history. They were originally manufactured for Russian carrier Transaero, but were never delivered after the airline collapsed. The US Air Force subsequently acquired the already-built 747-8s, and Boeing began the enormous job of transforming commercial widebodies into VC-25Bs. As The National Interest explains, the conversion requires major changes including presidential mission communications, an executive interior, a medical facility, self-defense equipment, upgraded electrical power, and autonomous ground-operation capabilities.

    Recent findings suggest that the result is considerably more complicated than installing a luxury cabin inside a 747, like they do with the BBJ variants. The VC-25B is effectively a national command-and-control military aircraft built within an existing commercial airframe, with systems that must function securely under demanding operating conditions. The current VC-25As entered presidential service in 1990, meaning the Air Force is simultaneously attempting to finish their replacements while sustaining aircraft whose basic 747-200 design dates to a much earlier era of commercial aviation.

    More recently, in September 2026, Gen. Dale White, the Air Force’s director of critical major weapon systems, stated Boeing would power up the lead VC-25B later this year, with a first flight to follow in 2027. Boeing CEO Kelly Ortberg has also said the company is investing heavily to keep its commitment to deliver the first aircraft in 2028.

    One of the most disruptive setbacks involved GDC Technics, which had been responsible for important interior work on the VC-25B. Boeing terminated the supplier in 2021 after alleging that delays in its performance were disrupting the overall program. Air & Space Forces Magazine reported that the resulting dispute and supplier problems contributed significantly to the program falling behind schedule.

    The interior of a presidential aircraft is also far removed from an ordinary airline cabin. Spaces must accommodate the president, senior advisers, Secret Service personnel, communications staff, journalists and other members of the traveling party while integrating highly specialized government equipment. Changing suppliers in the middle of such a colossal project involves considerably more than finding another tech giant capable of installing seats, partitions, and cabinetry.

    According to recent reports, the disruption came at an especially difficult moment. Boeing was simultaneously dealing with pandemic-related labor problems, inflation and supply-chain constraints across its businesses. Former Boeing CEO David Calhoun said in 2022 that COVID-related workforce problems, inflation and supply-chain disruption had affected several fixed-price defense programs, including VC-25B, according to another Air & Space Forces Magazine article. A problem that might have been manageable in isolation, therefore, became another bottleneck in an already extremely constrained production system, creating a snowball effect.

    Recent findings suggest that perhaps the biggest explanation for why the permanent VC-25Bs are taking so long is simply what Boeing is being asked to create. A standard Boeing 747-8 already contains an enormous network of electrical, hydraulic, environmental and avionics systems. The VC-25B must integrate an additional layer of mission-specific equipment without compromising the reliability, safety or maintainability of the underlying aircraft.

    The modification package includes mission communications, self-defense equipment, a distinguished-visitor interior, integral airstairs, autonomous baggage handling, a second auxiliary power unit and uprated electrical systems, according to Air & Space Forces Magazine's VC-25 overview. These modifications help explain why describing the VC-25B simply as a modified passenger 747 understates the engineering involved. Boeing must integrate systems developed for completely different purposes while ensuring that the completed aircraft remains certifiable, maintainable, and capable of performing the presidential airlift mission.

    Industry observers note that wiring has been a particularly stubborn concern. In Boeing’s 2024 financial reporting, the manufacturer noted a $250 million additional charge during the second quarter was driven partially by higher-than-expected costs associated with engineering design changes involving wiring and other structural requirements. Boeing's annual report subsequently disclosed another $129 million charge later in 2024 related to engineering design changes and schedule delays. More recently, the Government Accountability Office identified wire-bundle fabrication, detailed interior design and rework needed to correct defects in structural modifications as continuing schedule risks.

    Aircraft manufacturing is normally constrained by the availability of engineers, mechanics, components and factory capacity. VC-25B adds another requirement: many of the people working on sensitive areas of the aircraft need appropriate security clearances. That sharply reduces the available labor pool and means Boeing cannot necessarily move workers, including high-skilled ones from abroad, onto the program as easily as it could when trying to accelerate production of a commercial 737 or 787.

    Industry observers note that the concern has persisted for years. The Air Force has cited shortages of properly cleared personnel alongside supply-chain disruption as vital contributors to the program’s delay. Encouragingly, the latest GAO assessment noted that Boeing had made progress by hiring more qualified mechanics, according to Bloomberg. But adding personnel does not immediately erase accumulated schedule pressure, particularly when specialized workers must address unfinished work and rework while new systems are still progressing through design and certification.

    The challenge is magnified by the relatively tiny size of the program. Boeing is building only two permanent VC-25Bs, so it cannot spread development costs or learning across hundreds of aircraft in the way a commercial manufacturer does with a large production program. Every modification is effectively unique, and lessons learned on the first aircraft have limited opportunities to generate economies of scale beyond the second jet.

    Industry observers note that why has Boeing absorbed such extraordinary losses instead of simply passing higher costs to its customer? The answer lies in the contract. Boeing’s agreement is a firm fixed-price arrangement worth approximately $4 billion for engineering, development and modification of the two aircraft, meaning the manufacturer bears much of the financial consequences when the work costs substantially more than anticipated.

    In a recent development, boeing has repeatedly recorded additional charges as engineering, supplier and labor problems have accumulated. Its filings show a $482 million charge in 2023, followed by another $379 million during 2024 and a new $280 million charge in Q2 2026. Earlier charges included a $660 million hit revealed in 2022. The manufacturer has continued warning investors that additional losses remain possible, while its SEC filings describe VC-25B as a roughly $4 billion fixed-price program.

    Two Boeing 747-8 Intercontinentals.

    Labor, suppliers, wiring, structural rework, interior design.

    Permanent VC-25Bs delivered as of 2026.

    Recent findings suggest that the contract structure was initially attractive to the government because it limited taxpayer exposure to Boeing’s execution problems, but it has proved painful for the manufacturer. Boeing has absorbed billions of dollars in cumulative charges and continues to warn that more could follow. Importantly, that financial reality does not mean Boeing can simply abandon quality requirements to recover the schedule: a presidential aircraft has unusually high reliability, security and mission requirements, making schedule acceleration fundamentally different from speeding up delivery of a conventional airliner.

    Sources indicate that the obvious question is whether the arrival of another 747-8 has made Boeing’s delayed aircraft unnecessary. It has not. The US government accepted a former Qatari Boeing 747-8 as an interim presidential transport and pursued an accelerated modification effort intended to bridge the gap between the aging VC-25As and the eventual permanent VC-25Bs. Defense News reported in May 2026 that the aircraft had completed its initial modifications and flight testing ahead of its planned summer debut.

    According to recent reports, that aircraft subsequently arrived at Joint Base Andrews for commissioning in June and carried President Trump for the first time on July 1. However, its accelerated conversion differs from the much deeper work being performed on Boeing’s two permanent VC-25Bs. Reporting in July indicated that some planned capabilities for the full next-generation aircraft were omitted from the fast-track Bridge conversion in order to get it into service sooner, while further upgrades are expected. Defense News reported on July 20 that additional work was planned for the interim aircraft following questions about its security capabilities.

    The permanent VC-25Bs, therefore, remain central to the long-term presidential airlift mission. Current planning puts their deliveries around mid-2028 and mid-2029, but even those dates carry risk: GAO has highlighted unfinished interior designs, wire-bundle fabrication and structural rework among the remaining schedule concerns. After supplier failures, pandemic disruption, clearance-related labor shortages, engineering redesigns and billions of dollars in Boeing charges, the defining challenge is no longer merely getting a pair of 747s airborne. It is completing two aircraft capable of functioning as secure, survivable flying White Houses for decades to come, without creating yet another major schedule reset.

    Now hiring: Staff to power Democrats’ probes

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1247 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that ranking member Jamie Raskin, D-Md., arrives at the Rayburn Building for a House Judiciary Committee hearing in February.
    • Democrats in Congress have promised to hit the ground running with sprawling oversight investigations in the new year, making the most of their coming majority.
    • In a recent development, that means staffing up major committees.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that ranking member Jamie Raskin, D-Md., arrives at the Rayburn Building for a House Judiciary Committee hearing in February. He will be a key player in leading oversight efforts next year — and so will Democratic staff. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    Democrats in Congress have promised to hit the ground running with sprawling oversight investigations in the new year, making the most of their coming majority.

    In a recent development, that means staffing up major committees. And for the dozens of attorneys and other aides preparing to take on a belligerent Trump administration that has cast Democratic oversight as potentially criminal, the job will come with extra scrutiny.

    Arya Hariharan, former chief oversight counsel to Sen. Richard J. Durbin on the Senate Judiciary Committee and now a partner at Holland & Knight, said the pressure will be on from day one.

    “Are you prepared to not sleep very much and know that every single thing you do is going to be scrutinized, every footnote, every comma?” Hariharan said.

    Still, the way Hariharan sees it, serving on the Hill is worth it. “I hope they all fall in love with it because it’s a lovely place to work,” she says of staffers headed there for the first time.

    The work done by attorneys and other staff in oversight probes can promptly become part of constitutional law. When Trump adviser Peter Navarro defied a subpoena from Democrats investigating the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol, it touched off debates about executive privilege and contempt of Congress. Probes of Hunter Biden led to similar court fights.

    Some questions have gone all the way up to the Supreme Court, like in Trump v. Mazars, when the House fought to access Trump’s business records during his first administration in furtherance of toughening up government ethics laws.

    It has been revealed that there’s every indication that pressure will continue in the new Congress. James Melendres, a partner at Snell & Wilmer, said Democrats are poised for aggressive oversight efforts, even if they know it could be tough to make headway against litigation resistant administration officials.

    “Democrats are going to have less than two years to show results. I think they are going to move really fast,” Melendres stated.

    Democrats will likely soon start to send out preservation letters to private companies, institutions and others they intend to probe in the fresh year, if they haven’t already, Melendres noted.

    “There may be significant pushback from the administration, from agencies and individual government officials who receive requests. I think third-party, nongovernment agencies and individuals are going to be high on the list for these committees,” he said.

    In addition to the hiring that happens over the next few weeks, House Democrats will have major decisions to make about chamber and committee rules for the upcoming Congress, including who will hold subpoena authority. And off-Hill observers will be watching closely.

    “For companies, for individuals and their counsel, mapping all of that is going to be a big part of the job between now and early January,” Melendres remarked.

    Industry observers note that lawmakers need to nail down funding levels for congressional committees and staff — the amount of money involved can make a big difference in how big investigations get. Major committees, and major investigations, take a large amount of staff and expertise to get going.

    For instance, the special House panel that investigated the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol spent about $14 million in less than 18 months, including for dozens of staffers.

    Standing committees, such as Oversight and Judiciary, take a good chunk of change, too. In 2025 the House spent $12.9 million on the House Oversight and Government Reform panel, and $13.1 million on the House Judiciary Committee.

    Sources indicate that those expenditures mean dozens of staff working long hours to review documents, send letters, send subpoenas and conduct interviews. Judiciary ranking member Jamie Raskin, D-Md., who is expected to serve as chair next year, said he wouldn’t get into specifics yet about how many resources the newly introduced Congress may devote to oversight efforts.

    “But we are talking about the most corrupt administration in the history of the United States, and this is an overwhelming and daunting task that faces us,” Raskin mentioned.

    The Trump administration itself has already signaled it intends to push back forcefully on congressional oversight efforts.

    Earlier this month, President Donald Trump described Democrats’ vows to investigate his administration as “extortion at the highest level” and called for the Justice Department to “look into this criminal act, immediately!”.

    Days later, the White House counsel sent a letter saying that subpoena threats from House Oversight ranking member Robert Garcia, D-Calif., and others “may cross the line into blatant criminality.”.

    Sources indicate that U.S. Attorney Aaron Reitz for the Southern District of Texas followed up with letters of his own to Sens. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn.; Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass.; and Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., urging them to preserve documents tied to their promised oversight.

    “The American people are entitled to freely associate without their elected officials terrorizing them with aggressive, harassing government action,” Reitz’s letter to Warren remarked.

    Members of the incoming majority have signaled they intend to defend themselves and their probes, and Blumenthal remarked he won’t be deterred by the letter.

    “There’s no way that I’m going to be intimidated or bullied. It would be laughable and ludicrous, but it is a clear abuse and misuse of prosecutorial powers and weaponization by the Department of Justice,” said Blumenthal, who serves as the top Democrat on the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations.

    As for Raskin, he called the White House counsel letter and other missives “absurd on its face.”.

    In a recent development, “I’m sure they would love to get into a whole series of letters and counter-letters and litigation. They’re trying to distract everybody from the fact that they just lost the worst landslide electoral repudiation in at least a half century in America, and so they’re going to pick a fight,” Raskin told reporters.

    Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., the likely incoming speaker, told reporters last week that he intended oversight efforts in his chamber to be led by Raskin and Garcia.

    Recent findings suggest that “We haven’t ruled anything in. We haven’t ruled anything out. We’re going to follow the facts. We’re going to apply the law. We’re going to be guided by the Constitution, and we’re going to let the chips fall where they may,” Jeffries said.

    Democrats have already publicly listed a handful of job postings for oversight staff and counsel, ranging from the Science to Armed Services to Judiciary panels, set to start early next year.

    According to recent reports, beyond those hires, House Democrats will have to make one major pick they haven’t yet declared — the House counsel. The position, first created in the 1970s, is hired by the majority and advocates for the chamber in court. That attorney, along with a group of bipartisan House leaders controlled by the majority, will steer the chamber’s legal strategy.

    In a recent development, in prior Democratic Congresses, that office has been active in court; Doug Letter frequently argued on behalf of the Democratic House majority seeking to enforce subpoenas on behalf of congressional committees. The position is held by Matthew Berry in the current Republican-controlled House.

    “I mean, I think a lot of people are interested in that job,” Raskin stated.

    #65479. Lufthansa Management Threatens To Massively Shrink Airline, Lay Off Employees

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1810 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Onemileatatime ↗ Open Full Page

    Lufthansa Management Threatens To Massively Shrink Airline, Lay Off Employees

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1810 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that lufthansa is the “flagship” airline of Lufthansa Group, yet somehow, is the least profitable airline in the whole organization.
    • In a recent development, unfortunately things haven’t turned out so great.
    • It has been revealed that how is that working out?
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that lufthansa is the “flagship” airline of Lufthansa Group, yet somehow, is the least profitable airline in the whole organization. 2026 was supposed to be an exciting turnaround year for Lufthansa, as it’s even the carrier’s 100th anniversary.

    In a recent development, unfortunately things haven’t turned out so great. Earlier this year, the carrier dealt with massive labor issues, and back-to-back-to-back strikes. Just a few months ago, the organization’s senior management claimed it wanted to turn over a new leaf with labor relations, and stop fighting with employees, so that it could find long term solutions.

    It has been revealed that how is that working out? Well, Lufthansa pilots are just days from possibly being able to strike again, no agreement has been reached for long term peace with employees, and management is threatening to massively shrink its mainline operation. In other words, it’s just another day at Lufthansa!

    According to recent reports, lufthansa and its pilots have been in negotiations for quite some time over the future of the company. As you’d expect, broadly speaking, negotiations revolve around pay and future flying opportunities. As you’d expect at any airline, employees want as much flying as possible, and as major of a fleet as possible, since that’s what maximizes their compensation.

    The issue with Lufthansa Group management is that the manufacturer’s solution to everything is to simply create upcoming, low cost subsidiaries. And if Lufthansa Group management doesn’t like the terms with its subsidiaries, then it just shuts down the subsidiaries and creates new ones.

    Sources indicate that so that brings us to the current issue. Essentially, Lufthansa’s problem is that the airline doesn’t make money on short haul flights, given high costs and intense competition. So we’ve seen the carrier increasingly outsourcing this flying to Lufthansa City Airlines, a subsidiary with lower operating costs, operating the same kinds of planes as you’ll see in the mainline fleet.

    Lufthansa is asking its pilots to accept wage freezes, and is promising a certain level of career development opportunities. Pilots aren’t happy with what’s being proposed, so what’s Lufthansa’s solution?

    Management is reportedly proposing a fresh blueprint to the supervisory board, which would see the core Lufthansa brand massively reduce its regional flying, and largely outsource this to lower cost operations, like Lufthansa City Airlines. The idea would be to make Lufthansa primarily a long haul airline, and then have much of the short haul flying be operated by a subsidiary.

    It has been revealed that lufthansa’s mainline fleet currently consists of 260+ planes, with another 120+ planes on order. One proposal would see the mainline fleet reduced to 100 long haul aircraft and 100 short haul aircraft, with other planes being assigned to Lufthansa City Airlines.

    One radical proposal could even see Lufthansa exclusively have a long haul fleet and ditch short haul flying, though it’s noted that this isn’t the most likely scenario, and it could take several years for something like that to be implemented.

    Keep in mind that going back to 2017, Lufthansa had guaranteed pilots a minimum fleet size of 325 aircraft, but it terminated that agreement at the end of 2021. So it’s really hard for employees to trust any promises by management, when they can just be terminated.

    It has been revealed that there’s no denying that labor relations can be incredibly challenging, and that the economics of intra-Europe flying are also tough, when you have competitors like Ryanair, though Lufthansa doesn’t face nearly as much competition on that front as other carriers. Then again, Frankfurt (FRA) and Munich (MUC) aren’t exactly massively leisure destinations either.

    Most airline employees want their tech giant to succeed, and just want to be compensated fairly. Admittedly economics don’t always align. But what I find incredibly toxic is the approach taken by Lufthansa management. Let’s compare it to a marriage (which I think is a fair way to view the relationship between management and employees, since they’re “stuck” with one another).

    Lufthansa’s approach is to constantly threaten employees by saying that “if you don’t do what we want, we’ll just get rid of you.” That’s simply not a good faith way to approach things. Why would Lufthansa employees trust management, when they’ve repeatedly torn up contracts, and shown employees they simply don’t care? It would be like threatening to leave your spouse every time you have an matter, rather than trying to find a solution.

    Nothing against Lufthansa Group CEO Carsten Spohr personally, but I don’t understand how the board thinks he’s the best person for the job. Where’s the accountability for the endless management mistakes that have horribly impacted Lufthansa’s bottom line? Lufthansa’s employees are paying the price for the lack of success that comes as a result of all of Lufthansa’s errors, from the botched Allegris rollout, to Lufthansa’s very bad luck with newly introduced aircraft orders.

    And before anyone states “oh, but the unions,” contrast what has happened at Lufthansa Group to what has happened at Air France-KLM, under the leadership of Ben Smith. Smith has now been CEO at Air France for over eight years, and there hasn’t been a single strike under his leadership. Under the previous Air France-KLM CEO, there were endless strikes, and the situation got so bad that senior executives were being chased up a fence and having their clothes ripped off.

    According to recent reports, this shows that good labor relations absolutely can happen, balancing the needs of employees and the company. But it requires showing employees that you actually care about the company and their future. What was one of Smith’s first orders of business when he took the job at Air France-KLM? He eliminated Joon, the low cost carrier at the airline that was supposed to basically be a labor arbitrage opportunity. That was a way to show employees how much he respected them, and that he wanted a fair agreement, rather than one that would undermine them.

    Meanwhile Spohr’s solution to literally everything is to just threaten to start newly introduced subsidiaries or shut down existing subsidiaries. The irony is that Spohr started his career as a pilot, so you’d think he’d have respect for employees, having been on the other side. But clearly once he became senior management, his love for aviation turned into disdain for employees.

    A few months ago, Lufthansa management claimed it wanted to turn over a upcoming leaf when it comes to labor relations. That didn’t last long, because now the airline is back to its “do what we say or we’ll create a new subsidiary” approach.

    I don’t have a strong opinion on the exact negotiations as such. Obviously it’s a tough time for aviation, and intra-Europe flying is challenging. But if you ask me, the toxicity that has been created by Lufthansa management due to the lack of good faith negotiations just can’t be undone.

    If your only solution to everything is “oh, we’ll create a new subsidiary,” and if that doesn’t work, maybe it’s time for a new strategy. The fact that American CEO Robert Isom and Lufthansa Group CEO Carsten Spohr still have their jobs are two of the industry’s greatest mysteries.

    What do you make of Lufthansa’s latest threat to employees?

    The Bilt Palladium Card is one of my favorite credit cards, and it’s the card that gets the most of my spending. Just to cover some of the very basics, the card has a $495 annual fee (Rates & Fees), and offers the following value proposition at the moment:.

    Sources indicate that for me, the logic of picking up this card is pretty straightforward, and I’ve shared that in much more detail. The idea is that the combination of the 2x points plus 4% back in the form of Bilt Cash is an unrivaled return on spending, especially given the value of Bilt points.     On the most basic level, that Bilt Cash earns me 1x points per dollar spent on my housing payments (without any sort of fee), plus I take advantage of the Points Accelerator feature, which earns me an extra 1x points per dollar spent up to five times per year, by redeeming $200 in Bilt Cash. In other words, this card earns me 3x points on up to $25,000 of spending per year, plus I’m being rewarded on my housing spending.

    Points with Bilt rack up really swiftly, so if you spend quite a bit on credit cards, I do think this is tough to beat.     The good news is that through December 31, 2026, you can still opt into the old system for being rewarded, and that will then be honored in 2027 and beyond. This applies both to existing cardmembers, and those who pick up the card before then, and select this as their earnings preference.

    #65476. An Overhyped Trilateral Summit

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nationalreview ↗ Open Full Page

    An Overhyped Trilateral Summit

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (948 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nationalreview

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Donald Trump, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin have now concluded their first-ever trilateral meeting.
    • Recent findings suggest that that is not to deny that some of the optics involved were grating.
    • The fact that Putin was in the room has attracted criticism for its symbolic “confirmation” of Russia as one of, to borrow a term from the real Yalta, the “major three.” Not so much: Putin’s presence merely reflected geopolitical reality, something that, however unpleasant, cannot be wished away.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Donald Trump, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin have now concluded their first-ever trilateral meeting. Each leader has pronounced himself satisfied with their discussion. But if their concluding statement is an accurate reflection of what was said in the closed session, little of any real consequence — with one possible exception — was agreed to, which was only to be expected. Much has been made by some of the symbolism of the meeting. Did it signal that a disreputable carve-up, even a new Yalta, was underway? If that was the initiative, the result, appropriately and mercifully, looks like a package with more than a touch of Temu about it.

    Recent findings suggest that that is not to deny that some of the optics involved were grating. Trump’s earlier, overly enthusiastic greeting of his “friend” Putin — the aggressor, after all, in a genocidal war — was not only nauseating but also careless. It sent a disturbing signal to the rest of NATO, an organization that still plays a critical role in maintaining American security as well as peace, however uneasy, in Europe west of Ukraine. It is to be hoped that Trump’s delight at the sight of his supposed pal was, to use a word often applied to this president’s approach to diplomacy, transactional, a display of a dealmaker’s schmooze and nothing more.

    The fact that Putin was in the room has attracted criticism for its symbolic “confirmation” of Russia as one of, to borrow a term from the real Yalta, the “major three.” Not so much: Putin’s presence merely reflected geopolitical reality, something that, however unpleasant, cannot be wished away. Russia is economically enfeebled and embroiled in a brutally and humiliatingly debilitating war, but it remains a vast, resource-rich country that, militarily anyway, counts as a superpower and one that, as Ukrainians can testify, is still capable of wreaking immense destruction. The more interesting symbolism was detectable in the various gestures through which Xi Jinping emphasized during Putin’s visit that Russia is China’s junior partner. That, too, is today’s reality.

    As alluded to above, the joint statement issued after the meeting was, as should have been expected, thin gruel. There was talk of reforming the U.N. “so that it may respond more effectively to global challenges and fulfil its fundamental mission of maintaining international peace and security.” If that implies reining in Turtle Bay’s efforts to extend supranational (and thus post-democratic) governance, that’s no bad thing, but in practice little will probably change.

    In a similar vein, the trio, whose countries have not submitted to the jurisdiction of the International Criminal Court, implicitly criticized the attempted extension of its reach. They stressed the need for “respect for immunities of State officials,” a subject doubtless close to Putin’s heart. There is no need to grumble too much about this. The ICC is highly politicized, and, while it does not constitute much of a deterrent, it may even provide a perverse incentive to wrongdoers to hang onto power. Putin deserves to face judgment, but a better place for that would be Kyiv, not The Hague.

    And all three declared that they planned “to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations.” If that reflected some post-midterms unease on Trump’s part, that, as an admission of weakness, would have been a message better not sent. It would also be a mistake, despite recent waivers, for the U.S. to abandon its general application of sanctions on Iranian and Russian oil (the Europeans, incidentally, could do a better job of enforcing theirs). No pressure should be put on Ukraine to stop attacking Russian energy infrastructure other than as part of a general “energy cease-fire” such as that floated earlier this year, which Ukraine was willing to accept.

    According to recent reports, no details have been released so far of what was stated in the meeting about Ukraine. However, Putin has been reiterating his hard line, supplemented by an absurd and aggressive proposal to rewrite Europe’s security architecture. Hopefully, Trump was not misled by any bonhomie in Shenzhen, although some accounts of his later call with European leaders were not entirely encouraging in that respect.

    According to recent reports, from left: Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and U.S. President Donald Trump participate in a trilateral meeting during the APEC Economic Leaders’ Meeting in Shenzhen, China, November 19, 2026.

    To return to reality: China has no interest in helping end the war in Ukraine, and Russia’s ambitions in Europe are such that the eventual consequences of undermining Kyiv’s ability to resist won’t stop at Ukraine’s borders. Speaking of which, we hope that Trump warned Xi and Putin that the growing intensity of “gray zone” activity, from drones in Leipzig Airport to cyberattacks on both sides of the Atlantic, risks triggering retaliation that could easily spiral into something extremely dangerous.

    It has been revealed that any claims that the Shenzhen meeting has delivered the death blow to the post-1945 order would be overblown, akin to complaining about the murder of a corpse. The postwar settlement has been in flux for decades — Nixon, after all, went to China — a process that has accelerated, along with dramatic shifts in relative global economic and political power, since the Soviet collapse. But although the landscape has changed, Trump should pay more attention to America’s successful management of the (first) Cold War. Alliances matter, deterrence works, strength is rewarded, and aggression by, or sponsored by, hostile powers and their proxies should be contained and, where possible, reversed.

    The Editors comprise the senior editorial staff of National Review magazine and nationalreview.com.

    On “An Overhyped Trilateral Summit”.

    💡 Key Takeaways

    • People are increasingly using AI for travel planning, but here’s an interesting twist on that.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    There’s no denying that AI holds a lot of potential to transform how we go about our every day life, both for better or worse.

    People are increasingly using AI for travel planning, but here’s an interesting twist on that. Can AI help you find award flights and secure upgrades? It’s something I’d like to study in a bit more detail and write about in the coming weeks, but I just saw a post on Instagram that piqued my interest, so I figured it would make for a fun story. Consider this just a little teaser, for the time being.

    An Instagram user with 1.5 million followers who promises to help people master AI has just published a video about how “ChatGPT upgraded me to first class.” Now, that’s not as exciting as it sounds on the surface. The idea is simply that ChatGPT helped someone secure an upgrade through the standard means — it’s not like ChatGPT used his/her/their charm to sweet talk someone into an upgrade by dressing up nicely. 😉.

    Let me actually just quote the description of the video, which covers most of the content:.

    What happens when you ask ChatGPT to upgrade your flight to first class?

    I tried this on my flight in two weeks and it actually worked.

    Industry observers note that go to ChatGPT and switch from Chat to Work at the top. Start a upcoming chat and give it your airline and confirmation code.

    Prompt 1:“Ask me every question you need about my credit cards, my miles, and my memberships, and map out every upgrade currency I own for this exact flight.”.

    ChatGPT shows you that you’ve been sitting on upgrade power this whole time without even knowing it.

    Prompt 2:“Now look up my exact flight, check how empty the first class cabin is, and tell me every way I can get up there, ranked from free to cheapest.”.

    Prompt 3:“Now go get me the upgrade. Use my miles if the math is worth it, and place the upgrade bid at the smartest number, or get me on the upgrade list right now.”.

    ChatGPT opens its own browser, logs into your airline, and actually chases that seat for you while you sit back and do nothing.

    You can watch the video for yourself below.

    A post shared by Maverick Maltin | AI & ChatGPT (@mavgpt).

    Sources indicate that I don’t want to suggest AI isn’t useful, but I’d say that the example given is actually very poor. First of all, let’s be clear about what’s actually going on here. He had booked a business class ticket on American from Los Angeles (LAX) to London (LHR), and then upgraded to first class.

    Now, in the first place, something isn’t fully accurate here:.

    Okay, maybe he edited the dates, or something, which is fine, and it’s besides the point, but as a detail oriented airline nerd, I couldn’t help but notice those things. Anyway, let’s assume this is all accurate:.

    To me, this is kind of where AI falls flat, and it isn’t the correct way to use it. The prompt was reportedly to “use my miles if the math is worth it, and place the upgrade bid at the smartest number, or get me on the upgrade list right now.” This is where I get confused — you’d think that AI would be able to scour reviews online, and see that American first class isn’t (well, or wasn’t) really viewed as a product that’s worth the premium.

    If AI were really providing useful advice here, it would’ve recommend waitlisting with the systemwide upgrade, and otherwise recommending the guy save his 70,000 miles, and use them for something else. While there are definitely some strong use cases for AI, I think this is actually a pretty poor showing of what it can do.

    By the way, keep in mind that under United’s updated contract of carriage, using AI to help service reservations is banned, and could potentially get your ticket canceled. Whether there’s any enforcement of that remains to be seen.

    Recent findings suggest that while the thought of using AI to score an upgrade might sound great, don’t count on it actually getting you the best deal. An AI whiz claims he has the secret to using AI to upgrade to first class. All AI did was use the instant upgrade offer that was available directly on American’s website, and it didn’t even encourage him to skip the upgrade due to it not being worthwhile, or waitlisting the upgrade with a systemwide upgrade, which is objectively a much better deal than 70,000 miles.

    Latino voters moved sharply away from Republicans this year, and a record number of Latino Democratic candidates were elected.

    But California Rep. Linda T. Sánchez has a warning for her fellow Democrats.

    “Latino voters gave Democrats a two-year lease, but it expires in 2028 unless the party changes its playbook for good,” said Sánchez, who leads the campaign arm of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus.

    Failure to address rising costs and push back against President Donald Trump’s immigration agenda could once again scramble the political calculus and spark another realignment in two years, said House Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar of California.

    “While Latinos shifted towards Democrats and … gave us this mandate as a party, Democrats must continue to earn their trust, not just every two years, but every single day,’’ he said.

    Leaders of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus joined newly elected Latino members on Tuesday for a news conference to celebrate the recent wins and the role the group played in securing the House majority for Democrats. The caucus will boast 55 members in the next Congress, its largest roster ever, according to Sánchez.

    BOLD PAC, the caucus’ campaign arm, invested heavily in Latino candidates this year, including in primaries.

    In a recent development, california Rep. Salud Carbajal noted that BOLD PAC raised more than $18.5 million this cycle, which helped candidates leverage outside money.

    Working-class majority-Latino districts in South Texas, Arizona and California were among the areas that provided Democrats with their biggest wins. Democrats capitalized on voter dissatisfaction over rising costs, the very concern that helped Trump and the GOP make significant gains among Hispanic voters just two years earlier.

    But the wins weren’t limited to districts with sizable Latino populations.

    Rep.-elect Denise Powell, who flipped a swing seat in Nebraska, credited BOLD PAC for playing a key role in her win.

    “Yes, there are Latinos in Omaha, and those Latinos actually helped decide this race,’’ she stated. “BOLD believed in me as a candidate, but they also believed in our community.”.

    Rep.-elect Bobby Pulido, who came to politics after a successful career as a Latin Grammy-winning Tejano singer, flipped a redrawn South Texas border district that Trump would have carried by 18 points in 2024.

    “A lot of people feel like they don't belong to either party. But there's one thing about Latinos is we belong to each other,’’ Pulido said. “It's very hard to be a Latino right now in this country. … I expect to see us united, more united than ever, because it's a tough time right now.”.

    It has been revealed that several of the winning candidates deployed novel strategies to reach voters. Pulido famously began performing at quinceañeras after his Republican opponent dismissed him as a performer.

    In a recent development, colorado Rep.-elect Manny Rutinel, who flipped a battleground district north of Denver, attended World Cup and Broncos watch parties. “If people don't hear our message, then it doesn't matter,’’ he remarked.

    Industry observers note that the candidates “met those voters where they were,’’ Sánchez said. “They went into those communities and interacted in a very real and meaningful way. That's something I think that strategists or consultants don't always get. It's not just about pumping out lots of television commercials.”.

    In a recent development, amid those successes for Latino Democrats, Florida, home to one of the largest Latino electorates in the country, was a different story. Republicans held all three majority-Latino districts in the Sunshine State, though former news anchor Eliott Rodriguez, the son of Cuban immigrants, came within half a percentage point of unseating GOP Rep. María Elvira Salazar in a district that backed Trump by 15 points in 2024.

    BOLD PAC did have a victory to celebrate in Florida, with Rep. Darren Soto, the deputy chair of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus, narrowly prevailing in a district that Republicans redrew as one that no longer had a Latino majority.

    “The redistricting wars ended up failing because of the investment by BOLD PAC,’’ Soto noted.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • United Airlines is one of the world's top operators of narrowbody twinjets from the Boeing 737 MAX family, with fleet data from ch-aviation showing it at the moment has 123 737 MAX 8s and 188 737 MAX 9s.
    • Recent findings suggest that however, as times change for United's fleet, the same is true for its network.
    • Starting on the East Coast, Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR) has got off relatively lightly, with the MAX being removed from just two international routes.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    United Airlines is one of the world's top operators of narrowbody twinjets from the Boeing 737 MAX family, with fleet data from ch-aviation showing it at the moment has 123 737 MAX 8s and 188 737 MAX 9s. Going forward, the Chicago-based US 'significant three' legacy carrier and Star Alliance founding member is set to receive 35 more 737 MAX 9s as its mainline fleet modernizes.

    Recent findings suggest that however, as times change for United's fleet, the same is true for its network. When we compare the airline's 2027 schedules with those for 2026 (per data from Cirium, an aviation analytics manufacturer), we can see that it has taken the MAX off no fewer than 27 international routes. These are spread across six hubs: two on the East Coast, two on the West Coast, and two in the center of the US.

    Starting on the East Coast, Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR) has got off relatively lightly, with the MAX being removed from just two international routes. One of these serves Piarco International Airport (POS) in Trinidad, while the other links Newark with Vancouver International Airport (YVR) in Canada. This facility has also lost United MAX flights from another East Coast hub: Washington Dulles International Airport (IAD).

    United Airlines' East Coast Hubs.

    It has been revealed that as it happens, Vancouver is one of three Canadian destinations to have lost United MAX flights from Dulles, with the others being Calgary International Airport (YYC) and Toronto Pearson International Airport (YYZ). Elsewhere on the international front, 2027 will see the carrier stop flying its narrowbody twinjets from the 737 MAX series to Barbados, Liberia, or Nassau in the Caribbean.

    Moving west to United's two main hubs in the center of the US, cuts have also been made to the airline's foreign 737 MAX flights from Chicago O'Hare International Airport (ORD) and George Bush Intercontinental Airport (IAD). Canada remains a common theme, with O'Hare losing United MAX flights to Montreal Trudeau International Airport (YUL) and, again, Vancouver.

    These represent two of the four cuts in Chicago, with the others being Philip S.W. Goldson International Airport (BZE) in Belize City and the aforementioned Nassau. As for Houston, this is the airport where United has removed the MAX from the most routes, with eight corridors in total. Once again, two of the destinations are Canadian: Calgary and YYZ.

    In a recent development, as for the rest, three Mexican destinations are also included: Cozumel, San Jose Del Cabo, and Puerto Vallarta. The remaining trio are Caribbean destinations: Flamingo International Airport (BON) in Kralendijk on Bonaire, Owen Roberts International Airport (GCM) near George Town on Grand Cayman, and Santo Domingo Airport (SDQ) in the Dominican Republic.

    According to recent reports, united's two main West Coast hubs are both located in California. They are San Francisco International Airport (SFO) to the north and Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) to the south. Each will see the MAX removed from three international routes in 2027, with LAX losing flights to Puerto Vallarta, Toronto Pearson, and Vancouver.

    It has been revealed that vancouver will also disappear from United's MAX roster in San Francisco, with the other routes that are set to meet this fate serving Calgary and Tocumen International Airport (PTY) in Panama City. With that being stated, United will still retain considerable MAX networks from both of its West Coast hubs. In the 12 months to October 2027, it has planned 26,868 MAX flights from SFO and 11,132 from LAX.

    According to recent reports, united Airlines' use of the 737 MAX 8 and 9 is defined by a two-class setup with reasonable premium capacity. According to the airline, its MAX 9s have 20 domestic first/business class recliners and 159 economy seats on board (45/48 with extra legroom). Meanwhile, the smaller MAX 8 seats 16 domestic first/business class and 150 economy passengers (54 with extra legroom).

    • In an unprecedented trilateral summit in China this week, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin sat down with President Donald Trump. Ahead of the summit, Trump set no metrics for observers to judge its success. The summit cannot be said to have failed: It was not designed to achieve anything, and it didn’t. Of course, the president reportedly went into the diplomatic event of the year with some goals in mind. He reportedly sought commitments to nuclear disarmament from his Russian and Chinese counterparts, neither of whom had an incentive to agree to such limits. If Trump persuaded them to assist America’s efforts to isolate Iran economically, he has kept it a closely guarded secret. Putin sought to make the summit all about his war on Ukraine, but the Russian autocrat secured no meaningful promises on that front from Washington or Beijing. Only China, it seems, got what it wanted from the summit, which took place on its soil. The event allowed Xi to pretend to arbitrate the conflicts in which his great-power competitors are embroiled. The affair was not entirely unproductive, of course. It produced many joint statements of principle, which essentially state that all parties have agreed to keep talking.

    NR Editors includes members of the editorial staff of our magazine and website.
