    #65468. We Tracked 133 Diverted Flights In Two Weeks: Here’s Where They Ended Up

    📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1645 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    We Tracked 133 Diverted Flights In Two Weeks: Here’s Where They Ended Up

    📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1645 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that flight diversions are often treated as isolated incidents, but a closer look at two weeks of aviation activity reveals a much larger pattern.
    • Simple Flying Flight Tracker data examined 63 diversion posts covering 133 flights, including 17 major diversion waves involving four or more aircraft from the same airport within an hour.
    • Thursday, November 12, was easily the busiest day in our tracking period, accounting for 35 of the 63 diversion posts.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that flight diversions are often treated as isolated incidents, but a closer look at two weeks of aviation activity reveals a much larger pattern. Between November 6 and 18, 133 flights diverted from their intended destinations, and several airports saw multiple waves of diversions within hours. Some aircraft landed relatively close to their original destinations, while others ended up thousands of kilometers away.

    Simple Flying Flight Tracker data examined 63 diversion posts covering 133 flights, including 17 major diversion waves involving four or more aircraft from the same airport within an hour. From an 11-flight disruption at New York-JFK to a 13-aircraft scramble at San Francisco International Airport (SFO), the data reveals which airports absorbed the most diverted traffic, where airlines sent their aircraft, and which journeys experienced the most dramatic changes.

    Thursday, November 12, was easily the busiest day in our tracking period, accounting for 35 of the 63 diversion posts. The disruptions were particularly concentrated around Fresh York, where John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) saw an 11-flight diversion wave, along with numerous additional diversions involving transatlantic arrivals.

    Recent findings suggest that the disruption was noticeable among international operators. Aircraft arriving from Europe were redirected to airports across the northeastern United States, with Boston Logan International Airport (BOS) becoming the most frequently used alternative. Other aircraft were diverted to Bradley International Airport (BDL) in Connecticut, Philadelphia International Airport (PHL), Providence, and, of course, Bangor International Airport (BGR) in Maine, which has historically been a major diversion hotspot for many transatlantic flights. The diversions affected flights operated by several major airlines, including American Airlines, Delta Air Lines, British Airways, Air France, Lufthansa, and KLM Royal Dutch Airlines.

    The JFK disruption was not the only significant event that day. The neighboring Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR) experienced a four-flight diversion wave, while PHL saw eight flights redirected. LaGuardia Airport (LGA) also recorded four diversions. Together, these events demonstrate how disruption at several airports in the same metropolitan region can create a complicated situation for airline operations. But with so many aircraft needing alternative landing locations, which airports handled the most diversions?

    It has been revealed that boston was the most frequently used diversion airport during the tracking period, receiving 16 flights that had originally been scheduled to land elsewhere. Much of this traffic came from the November 12 disruption at JFK, when transatlantic arrivals were redirected to alternative airports across the northeastern United States.

    In a recent development, boston's geographical position made it a prominent destination in the diversion data. Several flights originally scheduled to land at JFK were redirected there, including services operated by American, Delta, British Airways, Air France, Emirates, and KLM. The affected routes included arrivals from London, Amsterdam, Paris Charles de Gaulle, Barcelona, Milan, and Dubai. However, Boston was not the only airport dealing with repeated waves of unexpected arrivals.

    On the other side of the Atlantic, Katowice International Airport (KTW) in Poland came remarkably close to the top, receiving 15 diverted flights. The airport became an vital alternative for aircraft originally scheduled to land at Krakow John Paul II International Airport (KRK), which experienced four separate diversion waves over four consecutive days. Back in the US, Fresno Yosemite International Airport (FAT) ranked third, receiving nine diverted aircraft, all tied to the major San Francisco disruption on November 18.

    Boston Logan International Airport.

    Fresno Yosemite International Airport.

    Washington Dulles International Airport.

    Los Angeles International Airport.

    Recent findings suggest that the geographical distribution is rather curious. Boston and Katowice were heavily affected by disruptions at nearby airports, while Fresno and Los Angeles benefited from their proximity to San Francisco. This raises another question: were these diversions isolated incidents, or were entire airports experiencing repeated operational disruptions?

    Krakow was one of the most interesting airports in the dataset, experiencing four separate diversion waves between November 6 and 9. Each wave involved at least four flights, with the aircraft redirected to several alternative airports across Poland and neighboring countries.

    The first wave occurred late on November 6, when four aircraft originally scheduled to land at Krakow were redirected. Three ended up at Katowice, while the fourth landed at Rzeszow-Jasionka Airport (RZE). The following morning, another six flights were diverted, with five heading to Katowice and one returning to Frankfurt. This included aircraft operated by Ryanair, Wizz Air, and Finnair, demonstrating that the disruption affected multiple airlines and aircraft types.

    The situation continued on November 8, when two further waves involved eight and five aircraft, respectively. Unlike the earlier events, these diversions were distributed across a wider selection of cities, including Warsaw, Wroclaw, Gdansk, Brno, and Ostrava. The final wave arrived on November 9, when another six flights were redirected, five of which landed at Katowice.

    Katowice, Warsaw, Wroclaw, Gdansk, Rzeszow, Ostrava.

    Wroclaw, Warsaw-Modlin, Brno, Lodz, Ostrava.

    According to recent reports, katowice's 15-flight total is particularly revealing because it shows how an airport can become an important alternative landing point during repeated disruption at a nearby facility. However, Krakow was not the only airport to experience a concentrated wave of diversions. On November 18, events unfolded on the opposite side of the Atlantic, producing the largest individual diversion wave recorded in our dataset.

    It has been revealed that on November 18, SFO saw the largest individual diversion wave in our tracking period, with 13 flights redirected in about an hour. Nine aircraft landed at Fresno, while another four were sent to Los Angeles International Airport (LAX).

    It has been revealed that the scale of the event was striking because it involved both domestic and international services. Among the affected aircraft was Korean Air flight 23 from Seoul Incheon (ICN), which landed in LAX instead SFO. Other long-haul services included United Airlines flight 862 from Hong Kong, which also diverted to LAX, and United flight UA34 from Osaka Kansai, which followed the same route.

    Recent findings suggest that domestic arrivals were affected too. JetBlue flight 633 from BOS and AA76 from JFK both landed at Fresno. DL668, arriving from JFK, was among the aircraft redirected to LAX. The nine-flight Fresno total made it the most frequently used alternative airport during the San Francisco event.

    The November 18 San Francisco diversion wave:.

    Fresno Yosemite International Airport (FAT).

    Los Angeles International Airport (LAX).

    Sources indicate that fresno's role and location are noteworthy. Although it is considerably smaller than San Francisco and Los Angeles, it absorbed most of the diverted aircraft in this event. This reveals how diversion planning can extend beyond a region's largest airports, depending on operational circumstances and available alternatives. However, the San Francisco wave was not the only event involving unusually long journeys to alternative airports. Some aircraft in our dataset ended up nowhere near their original destinations.

    Sources indicate that although many diversions involved relatively short journeys to nearby airports, several flights in our dataset experienced substantially longer route changes. The most dramatic example involved KL677, which was operating from AMS to Calgary International Airport (YYC).

    In a recent development, on November 9, the Boeing 787 operating the service landed at Keflavik International Airport (KEF), in Iceland, approximately 3,200 miles (5,132 kilometers) short of its intended destination. This was the longest diversion recorded in our dataset. The distance illustrates just how significant the operational consequences of a diversion can become when an aircraft is already deep into a long-haul journey.

    United Airlines flight UA114 experienced the second-longest diversion. The service was scheduled to fly from Papeete International Airport (PPT), in French Polynesia, to San Francisco, but instead landed at Honolulu International Airport (HNL). The aircraft arrived about (2,400 miles) 3,857 kilometers short of San Francisco, leaving passengers in Hawaii instead of the intended Californian destination.

    The third-largest diversion involved easyJet flight 7883, operating from AMS to Tenerife South Airport (TFS). Instead of reaching the Canary Islands, the aircraft landed at Paris Orly Airport (ORY), approximately 1,750 miles (2,814 kilometers) from its intended destination, much closer to the departure airport. The flight was unusual because it involved a European short-haul operator and a diversion just within 300 miles (about 500 km) of the departure point.

    The three longest diversions recorded:.

    These examples demonstrate that a diversion does not necessarily mean landing at the nearest available airport. Long-haul operations can involve complex considerations, and aircraft operating across different regions may have to use alternative airports far from their original destinations. But how representative are these individual examples of the overall diversion picture?

    The 133 flights recorded between November 6 and 18 provide an interesting snapshot of how swiftly disruption can spread across airline networks. Simple Flying's tracking identified 63 separate diversion posts, including 17 major waves in which at least four aircraft were diverted from the same airport within an hour. The dataset also contained 45 long-haul diversion posts and one short-haul diversion involving easyJet.

    It is crucial to distinguish between the number of posts and the number of flights. A single diversion-wave post could cover several aircraft, while individual long-haul diversions were also reported separately. Some long-haul flights were included in the larger waves, meaning the figures should not be added together as independent flight totals. ADS-B tracking independently confirmed the landing airports for every flight included in the spreadsheet.

    Simple Flying Flight Tracker's social channels regularly publish individual diversions and larger waves of disrupted flights as they happen. They offer a useful way to follow unexpected changes to airline operations in real time.

    Industry observers note that the most interesting finding isn't that 133 aircraft landed somewhere other than their planned destinations. It is how concentrated some of the disruption became. Boston absorbed 16 diverted flights, Katowice received 15, and Fresno handled nine aircraft during a single event at San Francisco. With individual waves involving as many as 13 aircraft, the data reminds us that an airport's operational importance can change dramatically when another facility is disrupted.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Presently, only United Airlines and Delta Air Lines operate the Boeing 767-400ER as a scheduled passenger aircraft, although a VIP-configured airframe also operates for the Bahrain Royal Flight (Bahrain Air Force).
    • These include being paid off (low capital and lease expenses); lower maintenance, tooling, and training expenses due to commonality with broader 757 and 767 fleets; and being able to fill very specific niches that no other aircraft on the market offers.
    • It has been revealed that delta is one of the world's largest airlines by several measures, with a mainline fleet of 1,009 aircraft, according to Planespotters.net.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Presently, only United Airlines and Delta Air Lines operate the Boeing 767-400ER as a scheduled passenger aircraft, although a VIP-configured airframe also operates for the Bahrain Royal Flight (Bahrain Air Force). While the -400ER is now a previous-generation aircraft with relatively high fuel consumption, it remains competitive within the Delta and United ecosystems for several reasons.

    These include being paid off (low capital and lease expenses); lower maintenance, tooling, and training expenses due to commonality with broader 757 and 767 fleets; and being able to fill very specific niches that no other aircraft on the market offers. Its closest modern equivalents are the 787-8 Dreamliner, the Airbus A330-800neo, and A330-900neo. That said, the A330-800neo almost doesn't count, as it's so unpopular that almost no airline is seriously considering it anymore. Here is what to know about where Delta is flying its 767-400ERs, according to data from Cirium, an aviation analytics company.

    It has been revealed that delta is one of the world's largest airlines by several measures, with a mainline fleet of 1,009 aircraft, according to Planespotters.net. It is also one of the primary remaining operators of the now-aging 767 family of passenger aircraft, with 57 examples in inventory. This is made up of 36 767-300ERs, whose average fleet age is now 29.7 years, and 21 767-400ERs with an average age of 26 years.

    It has been revealed that these were orders Delta placed itself. Delta inherited many aircraft from Northwest, but Northwest passed on the 767, citing its DC-10 fleet and cargo container compatibility—and instead chose A330-200s and A330-300s alongside its 747s and 757s. The 767-400ER was one of the least successful airliner variants Boeing has developed in modern times.

    In a recent development, boeing sold 1,451 examples of its 767 family, of which only 59 were the 767-400ER. It is unclear if Boeing ever recovered its expenses and broke even on the cost of developing the stretch. Regardless, the variant is now operated almost exclusively by Delta and United, for whom the aircraft fills a particular niche, making it difficult to replace. Both airlines apparently initiative to operate the type for as long as is feasible.

    According to recent reports, according to Cirium data, Delta is operating 12,308 flights with its fleet of 767-400ERs this year, including return flights. They carry a total of 2.9 million seats and generate about 11 billion available seat miles (ASMs). The average route distance is 3,245 nautical miles.

    In a recent development, the vast majority of these flights are operated from two Delta hubs: Hartsfield–Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL) and John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK). ATL has 2,934 outbound flights and 700,000 outbound seats, and JFK has 3,183 outbound flights and 758,000 outbound seats. There are some limited short-haul routes under 500 nautical miles from Atlanta, but not from JFK.

    Delta 767-400ER: Top 8 Routes By Frequency.

    New York – Paris Charles de Gaulle.

    The 767-400ER's regular routes are within the 2,000 to 4,300 nautical mile range, with the aircraft sometimes used to plug gaps on short routes or to run short routes between its longer-haul schedules. Overall, it is useful to think of the aircraft as a transatlantic workhorse as well as a lesser transcontinental workhorse. Only three pairings have more than 1,000 annual flights, and only one has more than 500 flights.

    Industry observers note that all of Delta's shortest 767-400ER routes under 1,000 nautical miles are from its Atlanta hub, ignoring the ATL-JFK pairing. The shortest route is Atlanta to Orlando at just 350 nautical miles, with a total of 62 flights in both directions (outbound and inbound) for the year. Just three nautical miles longer is the Atlanta to Tampa pairing, with 20 flights covering 353 nautical miles.

    Delta conducted eight flights between Atlanta and Detroit (516 nautical miles) and about 206 flights between Atlanta and Miami (517 nautical miles), meaning Florida dominates the shortest-route destinations. After Miami, the next shortest route is ATL to JFK, with 175 flights at 660 nautical miles. The only other destinations under 1,000 nautical miles are from Atlanta to Minneapolis-St. Paul at 787 nautical miles, although this route only sees four flights.

    In the 1,000-1,999 nautical mile category, from and to Atlanta, there are 136 flights with Phoenix (1,379 nautical miles), 20 flights with Las Vegas (1,518 nautical miles), four flights with San Diego (1,643 nautical miles), 145 flights with Los Angeles (1,691 nautical miles), and 12 flights with San Francisco (1,859 nautical miles). Besides Atlanta, there are two flights between New York-JFK and Phoenix (1,871 nautical miles) and a single flight from Las Vegas to New York (1,953 nautical miles).

    Sources indicate that moving above 2,000 nautical miles is the first very busy route, the transcontinental route between New York-JFK and Los Angeles with 1,617 flights at 2,151 nautical miles. JFK's 2,247-nautical-mile route to San Francisco sees 96 flights. The 767-400ER is one of the workhorses for Delta's transatlantic routes. It has the range to connect the East Coast with many of Western Europe's top destinations.

    Next, transatlantic routes start from JFK. There are 173 flights (including return) to Dublin (2,763 nautical miles), 80 to Edinburgh (2,829 nautical miles), 137 to Lisbon (2,926 nautical miles), and 423 to London Heathrow (3,000 nautical miles). Going over 3,000 nautical miles, JFK's transatlantic pairings include Madrid (436 flights), Paris (1,117 flights), Barcelona (200 flights), and Zurich (483 flights).

    It has been revealed that these destinations are between 3,120 and 3,416 nautical miles. Finally, Atlanta sees its first transatlantic route to Dublin with 78 total flights. The other flight pairings under 3,500 nautical miles include New York and Nice (430 flights), New York and Milan Malpensa (387 flights), and a single flight from Atlanta to Edinburgh. ​​​​​​​.

    Sources indicate that moving above 3,500 nautical miles, the first and only major route not to include Upcoming York or Atlanta is the 3,611-nautical-mile pairing between Cincinnati and Paris (250 flights). This is the same distance as Delta's New York to Venice pairing (451 flights). The next ten routes by distance (3,767 nautical miles to 4,132 nautical miles) are all from Delta's Atlanta hub.

    In order of distance, these are London Heathrow (1,527 flights), Madrid (288 flights), Marrakech (127 flights), Paris (426 flights), Brussels (187 flights), and Barcelona (198 flights). After Barcelona, the routes are greater than 4,000 nautical miles and include Zurich (292 flights), Rio de Janeiro (315 flights), Nice (306 flights), and Milan (387 flights).

    According to recent reports, the Atlanta-Rio de Janeiro pairing is the first non-European international destination by ascending distance. Delta also operates 18 flights on its Upcoming York-Rio de Janeiro pairing, which is only marginally longer than the Atlanta pairing. Next, there are 652 flights between Atlanta and Munich and 197 flights between Atlanta and Venice.

    In a recent development, the top five longest Delta 767-400ER routes are all over 4,250 nautical miles, but the frequencies are low. The New York-Athens pairing sees 135 flights over 4,294 nautical miles. Next is Atlanta to Buenos Aires with 95 flights. Delta typically assigns A330s and A350-900s on its Atlanta to Buenos Aires route. After Atlanta to Buenos Aires, there are no more regular flights.

    In a recent development, there are two flights between Las Vegas and London Heathrow, two flights between Upcoming York and Buenos Aires, and a single flight from Paris to Las Vegas. The latter is the longest flight at 4,730 nautical miles. Delta's A330-900neos are the primary aircraft serving the Buenos Aires-New York route. It seems that with these routes (as well as very short routes), the 767-400ER is occasionally used to fill in when the aircraft typically assigned to the route are lacking.

    According to Boeing, the 767-400ER has a basic range of 3,580 nautical miles and a 5,190 nautical miles range at maximum optional weight, with a 3% fuel factor. Judging by how Boeing is actually flying the aircraft, it is best suited for ranges from 2,000 nautical miles up to around 4,300 nautical miles. Most of Delta's 767-400ER's highest-frequency routes are transatlantic, with the notable exception of the New York-Los Angeles pairing and, to a much lesser extent, the New York-San Francisco route.

    Breaking: Jeffries puts immigration bill high on Democratic priority list

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (730 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that house Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., holds a news conference in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday.
    • House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries is signaling Democrats will move promptly on immigration legislation when the party reclaims the House in January, while acknowledging it still has work to do in shaping its healthcare agenda.
    • Jeffries, who is expected to secure his spot as the next speaker during a closed-door vote of the Democratic caucus Wednesday, identified immigration and health care as among the top priorities for the incoming majority during a Tuesday news conference.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that house Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., holds a news conference in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries is signaling Democrats will move promptly on immigration legislation when the party reclaims the House in January, while acknowledging it still has work to do in shaping its healthcare agenda.

    Jeffries, who is expected to secure his spot as the next speaker during a closed-door vote of the Democratic caucus Wednesday, identified immigration and health care as among the top priorities for the incoming majority during a Tuesday news conference.

    “One of the things that we need to do is to move the Dream and Promise Act for DACA recipients and TPS recipients,” Jeffries noted, referring to a Democratic bill introduced last year. “We should actually move that bill immediately.”.

    The proposal aims to create a path to citizenship for certain Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals recipients and Temporary Protected Status holders. Similar legislation has been a top priority for Democrats in both chambers for more than a decade, with Democrats unable to advance this bill in the House while Republicans have held the majority.

    Jeffries also reiterated his calls to rein in Immigration and Customs Enforcement and redirect funding allocated to the agency through Republicans' budget law known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, while expressing a desire for bipartisan cooperation on immigration more broadly.

    “We think the border should be safe and strong and secure, and we think our immigration system overall is broken,” Jeffries stated. “We need to fix it in a comprehensive way, and certainly, it's our hope that a handful of Republicans will be willing to join us, so we can fix it in a bipartisan way.”.

    On healthcare, however, Jeffries offered fewer specifics, suggesting Democrats still have decisions to make before taking control of the chamber. Democrats broadly agree on the need to restore subsidies for plans purchased through health insurance markets that expired at the end of 2025. But the question of what additional steps the party should pursue with the goal of expanding coverage and lowering prices is likely to be a major test of Democratic leadership’s ability to find consensus among its robust latest majority.

    When asked how far Democrats want to lower the Medicare eligibility age, Jeffries responded, “that's all part of an ongoing conversation.”.

    The Upcoming York Democrat outlined several broader healthcare priorities, including reversing Medicaid cuts enacted under President Donald Trump, extending Affordable Care Act tax credits, all of which Democrats have vowed to do over the last year.

    “Out of the gate, what we clearly have to do is fix our broken healthcare system in terms of the damage that's been done by Donald Trump and MAGA extremists over the last two years, and that clearly involves reversing the Medicaid cuts and extending the Affordable Care Act tax credits, and beginning to engage in supporting medical research, particularly things like research for pediatric cancer,” Jeffries added.

    Industry observers note that democrats established a healthcare working group earlier this Congress, led by Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y. and Terri Sewell, D-Ala., to gather perspectives and develop policy proposals as the party works toward a broader agenda.

    Recent findings suggest that without an announced challenger, Jeffries has expressed confidence that he’ll secure the top Democratic spot in the House, brushing aside questions about incoming members who have noted they remain “undecided” ahead of Wednesday’s elections. Jeffries, who was introduced as “Speaker Jeffries” on election night, said last week he was “very confident we’ll get there” and confirmed that the caucus will hold a recorded vote in the contest.

    Rep. Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., was nominated for speaker by acclamation ahead of her first election to the position in 2007. But Jeffries’ allies portrayed his decision to go forward with a recorded vote as a show of strength after a group of incoming progressives, many aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America, had floated forcing a recorded vote in the internal leadership race.

    Jeffries said Tuesday the approach mirrors the caucus’ 2018 transition from minority to majority, giving members an opportunity to weigh in on who is best positioned to lead based on “track record, experience and vision.”.

    Industry observers note that this report was corrected to reflect Rep. Nancy Pelosi’s status as a current member.

    Latest Update: Senators still see NDAA as chance for online safety legislation

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Josh Hawley, R-Mo., delivers his opening statement during the hearing on Tuesday.
    • Online safety advocates are looking to the annual defense policy bill for action on legislation to expand accountability for online platforms in cases of child sexual exploitation, as they also introduced legislation to make sure those cases aren’t forced into private arbitration.
    • Senators and advocates expressed support Tuesday for legislation that would expand the ability of victims of online sexual exploitation to sue social media platforms at a hearing focused on dangers children face on the gaming platform Roblox.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., delivers his opening statement during the hearing on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call).

    Online safety advocates are looking to the annual defense policy bill for action on legislation to expand accountability for online platforms in cases of child sexual exploitation, as they also introduced legislation to make sure those cases aren’t forced into private arbitration.

    Senators and advocates expressed support Tuesday for legislation that would expand the ability of victims of online sexual exploitation to sue social media platforms at a hearing focused on dangers children face on the gaming platform Roblox.

    The Senate Judiciary Committee’s panel on Crime and Counterterrorism held the hearing after its Chairman Josh Hawley, R-Mo., and ranking member Richard J. Durbin, D-Ill., introduced a bill Monday that would ban pre-dispute arbitration agreements from affecting cases where a minor was harmed online, including by sexual exploitation.

    Industry observers note that hawley and Durbin also worked together on a separate bill to expand eligibility for victims of abuse to bring civil suits against online platforms that intentionally, knowingly or recklessly promoted or facilitated the abuse. It would also include penalties for certain platforms that fail to report child pornography violations on their sites.

    That bill is included in a manager’s amendment to the Senate’s fiscal 2027 National Defense Authorization Act bill. Durbin encouraged Congress to pass the NDAA “in the closing days” of the session because “protecting children is an key part of it.”.

    “I have a few weeks left in my service in the United States Senate,” remarked Durbin, who is retiring at the end of his term in January. “I’m thinking each day it’s coming to an end, but I want it to come [to an] end the right way.”.

    The subcommittee has spent much of the 119th Congress focused on harms to children online, including from artificial intelligence chatbots.

    Tuesday’s hearing included testimony from survivors and experts on child exploitation on Roblox.

    Hawley noted that victims are bound by pre-dispute agreements with Roblox to settle claims through private arbitration, rather than in court.

    “They slam the courthouse door shut in their faces,” Hawley remarked. “We’re talking about children now, child victims of sexual exploitation online are denied their day in court by the very company that has exposed them to the content to begin with.”.

    A spokesperson for Roblox said in a statement that “safety has been central” to the platform since its launch.

    “We require age checks for chat, place users under 16 in age-based accounts with protective defaults, and block images and video in chat,” the spokesperson remarked. “A legal position about arbitration is not a measure of a company’s safety record, and a hearing built around it fails to advance safety.”.

    Myriam Gilles, a professor of law at Northwestern University, told the panel that a 2022 law that ended forced arbitration agreements for victims of sexual assault has gaps. She said Roblox has argued it does not apply to online actions, just “completed physical assault” and does not apply to platforms.

    She also mentioned that Hawley’s new arbitration bill would enhance the effects of his measure regarding civil suits by making sure those suits can be heard publicly if families so choose.

    Industry observers note that “Congress can pass laws, but if [suits] just get shunted into private arbitration, they’re doing no good in the world,” Gilles stated. “A right to sue that ends in secret arbitration is a right in name only.”.

    The hearing came the same day that advocates, including reality TV personality and activist Paris Hilton, held a press conference to urge House action on a bill (S 1837) that would allow individuals to bring civil suits over nonconsensual intimate depictions generated by artificial intelligence or for possession or production of deepfake porn if there was also intent to disclose the images.

    That bill passed the Senate in January but has not been taken up in the House.

    Link: Sign-up for a Rakuten account with a best-ever $50 bonus.

    According to recent reports, rakuten is a free online shopping and rewards platform that pays customers either cash back or points for the shopping they do online. Rakuten partners with over 3,500 online retailers, many of which are well known, ranging from Lowe’s, to Nike, to Target. The Rakuten shopping portal concept is simple — if you click through from Rakuten to the partner website, Rakuten tracks the purchase and gets paid a commission, and then you get a reward as well.

    Note that as a consumer, Rakuten is free to use. The commission is paid by the business, so you’ll pay the same price you’d pay if you just went directly to the retailer’s website. To maximize your savings, you can even download the Rakuten browser extension, which will automatically notify you when you can earn extra rewards.

    Sources indicate that I should mention that there are several online shopping portals out there to choose from, so Rakuten isn’t the only one. Personally I find that Rakuten is my favorite because it has among the largest selection of partners, it gives you the flexibility to earn cash back or points, and I also find the earnings rates to be very competitive.

    It can always pay to use a site like Cashback Monitor to compare the earnings rates for retailers across portals, so that you’re maximizing your rewards. In some situations you may be better off using other portals, so it’s always worth understanding what your options are.

    In a recent development, through December 31, 2026, Rakuten is offering a generous elevated refer-a-friend bonus. Specifically, if you refer a friend to Rakuten and they spend $50 within the first 90 days, then both the person referring and the person being referred each receive $50.

    Sources indicate that this is a very good deal. Essentially Rakuten is giving out $100 total for a $50 purchase, between the person referring and the person being referred. Long term you can potentially get even more value with Rakuten, as rewards can be converted into Amex or Bilt Points.

    Actually earning the $50 Rakuten sign-up bonus is really straightforward:.

    Recent findings suggest that what’s the timeline with which you’ll actually receive the rewards? With Rakuten you’re paid (either in cash or points) once quarterly, and there’s a cutoff for payments, per the below chart.

Much like Amex Membership Rewards points, I also value Bilt Rewards points at 1.7 cents each, as there are also many good uses of this points currency.

    What’s cool here is that your cash back can retroactively be converted into Bilt Points for the entire Rakuten “payout” period (roughly quarterly), and that means even the refer-a-friend bonus can be converted into points.

    Industry observers note that if you have the choice between one Amex point or one Bilt point, I think many people might prefer the latter, given the value of the rewards, plus how hard they are to earn.     Alaska Atmos Rewards Business Card Review: 90K Points & Strong Perks

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that the Atmos™ Rewards Visa Signature® Business Card is the business credit card of Atmos Rewards, which is the loyalty program of Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines.
    • It has been revealed that the card has just undergone a full refresh, and there are many reasons to consider picking up this card, especially if you fly Alaska or Hawaiian with any frequency.
    • Link: Learn more about the Atmos™ Rewards Visa Signature® Business Card.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that the Atmos™ Rewards Visa Signature® Business Card is the business credit card of Atmos Rewards, which is the loyalty program of Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines. The card is issued by Bank of America, and is a rebranding of the former Alaska Airlines Visa Business Card.

    It has been revealed that the card has just undergone a full refresh, and there are many reasons to consider picking up this card, especially if you fly Alaska or Hawaiian with any frequency. This post is my in-depth Atmos Rewards Business Card review, so I’d like to take a look at the card’s value proposition, for anyone who may be considering applying.

    Link: Learn more about the Atmos™ Rewards Visa Signature® Business Card.

    Before I get into my Atmos Rewards Business Card review, here’s a brief summary of the key details of the card:.

    Below are what I consider to be the pros and cons of the Atmos Rewards Business Card.

    The Atmos Rewards Business Card is the only business card in the Atmos Rewards ecosystem. To start, let’s cover the welcome bonus, card eligibility rules, annual fee, and more, since these are notable factors that cardmembers consider.

    Industry observers note that the Atmos Rewards Business Card is offering a limited time welcome bonus where you’ll get 90,000 bonus points after you make $6,000 or more in purchases within the first 90 days of opening your account. This is the best publicly available bonus that we’ve ever seen on the card, and you can find the bonus offer history in this post.

    In a recent development, based on my latest miles & points valuations, Atmos Rewards points are worth 1.5 cents each, given the great uses of these rewards. That means the 90,000 points are worth $1,350 for me.

    It has been revealed that the Atmos Rewards Business Card is issued by Bank of America. The good news is that eligibility for this card is unrelated to having any other Atmos Rewards card, so you’re eligible for this card (including the bonus) if you have the Atmos™ Rewards Ascent Visa Signature® credit card (learn more) or Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® Credit Card (learn more).

    Let me emphasize that you are eligible for this product if you have any of the previously issued personal or business HawaiianMiles Barclays cards, or any of the previously issued personal Alaska Mileage Initiative cards.

    Beyond that, Bank of America doesn’t have many consistent restrictions when it comes to getting approved for business cards. While Bank of America has the 2/3/4 rule and 3/12 rules, those apply to personal cards, and not business cards. Generally those with a Bank of America banking relationship also have the best odds of approval (though it’s by no means a requirement).

    Industry observers note that there’s not a consistent credit score you need to have to be approved for this card, though personally I’d hope to have a score in the “good” to “excellent” range, ideally 700+ points. However, people with lower scores have been approved, and people with higher scores have been rejected.

    Applying for this card won’t count as a further card toward Chase’s 5/24 limit, in case that’s a limit you’re trying to stay under.

    I should also mention the following restriction in the terms:.

    I also understand that I may be declined for additional credit card accounts if my business entity currently has, or has had, another business card with Bank of America in the preceding 24 month period.

    Industry observers note that on the surface, this suggests you may be declined for a Bank of America business card if you have another Bank of America business card. However, anecdotally, this doesn’t appear to be enforced much. I think the term “may” is the key here (which is different than “will”).

    Sources indicate that the Atmos Rewards Business Card has a $195 annual fee. That’s on the steep side, though the card does have some premium perks. The good news is that you can add employee cards at no extra cost, so that annual fee covers the cost for all the cards you’ll have.

    It has been revealed that the Atmos Rewards Business Card has bonus categories that can help you rack up points faster. Furthermore, spending on the card can help you earn Atmos Rewards elite status. Let’s talk about how rewarding spending on the card can be.

    The Atmos Rewards Business Card offers 10x points per dollar spent on flights booked through the Atmos for Business website. If you’re looking to maximize your earning, this is where you want to book your Alaska and Hawaiian flights, as this is an incredible deal.

    It has been revealed that you do need your own business to participate in the Atmos for Business program, and once registered, the return on spending is really tough to beat. Based on my valuation of points, that’s like an incremental 15% return on eligible airfare spending, on top of what you otherwise earn.

    The Atmos Rewards Business Card offers 3x points on all other eligible Alaska and Hawaiian purchases, with no caps. Based on my valuation of Atmos Rewards points, that’s like a 4.5% return on spending. So if you fly either of those Alaska Air Group carriers with any frequency, that’s a solid return on that spending.

    The Atmos Rewards Business Card offers 2x points on eligible dining purchases. Based on my valuation of Atmos Rewards points, that’s like a 1.5% return on spending. It’s always nice to earn bonus points, though in fairness, 2x points isn’t exactly the biggest return on spending that we’ve seen.

    The Atmos Rewards Business Card offers 1x points on all other eligible spending. Based on my valuation of Atmos Rewards points, that’s like a 1.5% return on spending. As you might expect, there are more exciting cards for everyday spending, as independently, that’s not a terribly exciting return.

    According to recent reports, the Atmos Rewards Business Card can help you earn elite status in the Atmos Rewards program. Specifically, the card offers one status point for every $3 in eligible spending. There’s no cap on how many status points you can earn with the card.

    If you are serious about earning status with spending, I’d recommend instead considering the Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® Credit Card (learn more), which offers one status point for every $2 in eligible spending.

    Beyond the ability to earn one status point per $3 spent, the Atmos Rewards Business Card offers some additional threshold bonuses for spending, including bonus status points and discount codes:.

    In other words, spending $200,000 per anniversary year would earn you 20,000 bonus status points, plus a discount code for 50% off a base fare. Just to cover the basics of that 50% off base fare discount code, here’s how that works:.

    Recent findings suggest that so the value of this will depend on how you’d usually travel, but this could easily save you many hundreds of dollars, depending on the type of ticket you book. It’s also still possible to upgrade these tickets, but at least the initial booking has to be in economy.

    It has been revealed that the Atmos Rewards Business Card also offers a Bank of America relationship bonus. If you have an eligible small business Bank of America checking or savings account, you’ll receive a bonus equal to 10% of the points you earn on each dollar spent.

    This is a way to earn even more rewards, as you’d earn 11x points on Atmos for Business purchases, 3.3x points on Alaska and Hawaiian purchases, 2.2x points on the other purchases eligible for bonus categories, and 1.1x points on everyday spending.

    The Atmos Rewards Business Card has no foreign transaction fees, so it’s a decent card to use for purchases abroad, since you can rack up rewards without paying a fee.

    In a recent development, the Atmos Rewards Business Card offers a variety of benefits and credits, which can potentially more than justify the annual fee year after year. These perks are the main reason you want to consider picking up this card, in addition to the great welcome bonus. In no particular order, let’s go over the main benefits.

    It has been revealed that the Atmos Rewards Business Card offers a free checked bag for you and up to six guests on the same reservation when flying on Alaska or Hawaiian. In order to be eligible for this perk, you need to charge the cost of the ticket to your card. Another great thing is that authorized users on the card can also receive this benefit, as long as their ticket is purchased with the card, so that’s a huge incentive to add authorized users to the card.

    This is a great benefit that could save you a lot of money — Alaska and Hawaiian ordinarily charge $30-45 per checked bag, so that’s a savings of up to $90 per person roundtrip, if checking bags. If you fly Alaska or Hawaiian fairly often but don’t have elite status, that alone could quickly more than justify the annual fee.

    The Atmos Rewards Business Card offers preferred boarding for you and up to six guests on the same reservation. In order to be eligible for this perk, you need to charge the cost of the ticket to your card. Another great thing is that authorized people on the card can also receive this benefit, as long as their ticket is purchased with the card.

    It has been revealed that this is a valuable benefit that helps you ensure that there’s space in the overhead bin for your bags. It’s also an awesome authorized user perk, so that you can share this benefit with others.

    According to recent reports, the Atmos Rewards Business Card offers four Alaska Lounge passes annually. The way this works, the primary cardmember will have one Alaska Lounge pass deposited into their Atmos Rewards account at the beginning of the quarter, valid through the end of the quarter.

    It has been revealed that each is valid for access to Alaska Lounges on a single calendar day, in conjunction with a same day flight operated by Alaska, Hawaiian, a oneworld airline, or an Alaska global partner. Each pass is valid for one adult, plus accompanying children. For what it’s worth, a day pass would otherwise cost $60 per person.

    According to recent reports, if you’re the primary cardmember on the Atmos Rewards Business Card, you can share your Atmos Rewards points with other members at no cost. The way this works, you can link your accounts with up to 10 other Atmos Rewards members (they don’t have to be family — accounts of friends are fine as well), and then you can move points back and forth for free.

    I’d argue that this is especially compelling for families, because it’s easier to rack up a sizable balance of points when you can consolidate them into one account.

    The Atmos Rewards Business Card offers 20% back on Alaska and Hawaiian inflight purchases when paying with your card. This applies for the purchase of food, beverages, and Wi-Fi onboard flights, and the statement credit should post to your account within seven days. There’s no limit to how often you can take advantage of this.

    Let me just mention that Alaska and Hawaiian should have free Starlink Wi-Fi fleetwide by some point in 2027, at which point there won’t be savings anymore with Wi-Fi. That being said, it can still be used for food and beverages.

    Recent findings suggest that if you’re the primary cardmember on the Atmos Rewards Business Card, then you’re eligible for a free same day confirmed flight change on Alaska. This ordinarily costs $50 per person, so that’s quite valuable.

    Sources indicate that with this, you can change to another flight that might be more convenient, subject to capacity controls. This is especially useful in high frequency markets.

    If you’re the primary cardmember on the Atmos Rewards Business Card, you’re eligible to receive a $50 voucher if you have an Alaska flight that is delayed by at least two hours, or that’s canceled within 24 hours of departure.

    The $50 voucher is valid for 48 hours, and will be delivered to the email address associated with the reservation, and can be used for food, drinks, etc. Travel must have been booked directly with Alaska using the eligible credit card.

    Those with the Atmos Rewards Business Card receive up to a $120 airport security credit every four years, in connection with TSA PreCheck or Global Entry. This is a perk offered by many premium credit cards, and there’s lots of value to this.

    When talking about an Atmos Rewards credit card, it’s worth acknowledging the general value in earning and redeeming Atmos Rewards points. Alaska & Hawaiian are both in the oneworld alliance, and Atmos Rewards partners not only with oneworld partner airlines, but also with all kinds of other unaligned airlines. I consider Atmos Rewards to be one of the most valuable points currencies out there.

    Sources indicate that atmos Rewards has a distance based award chart, which varies a bit by region. For example, below is the one-way award chart within the Americas.

    Sources indicate that I constantly redeem Atmos Rewards points for travel within the United States, particularly on American. For example, all the time I redeem 4,500 points to fly one-way economy from Miami to Tampa (when cash fares would often be $200+), or 15,000 points to fly one-way business class from Miami to Chicago or New York (when cash fares would often be $500+). You simply can’t beat these redemption rates.

    The icing on the cake is that with Atmos Rewards, you earn status points for award flights, so those flights even count toward elite status, and that’s also why I’ve switched my business to Atmos Rewards.

    Of course there are lots of other opportunities with Atmos Rewards points as well. For example, I love the ability to redeem 75,000 points for one-way business class from the United States to many parts of Asia on carriers like Japan Airlines or Starlux Airlines — those are both awards that I’ve booked for myself in the past, and they were a great value.

    What makes this an even better value is that you can have a free stopover on a one-way award when traveling long haul. One thing worth being aware of is that Atmos Rewards has a $20 per person per direction partner award booking fee. However, that can be waived if you have the Atmos Rewards Summit Card.

    Sources indicate that the Atmos Rewards Business Card is the only business card in the Atmos Rewards ecosystem, so how valuable is this product? A few thoughts….

    First of all, I think there’s a lot of merit to picking up this card for the excellent welcome bonus, which includes a lot of points. The card also has significant ongoing benefits. The card also doesn’t count toward the Chase 5/24 limit, which is nice. Given the value of the Atmos Rewards ecosystem, there’s no reason not to pick up this card, if eligible.

    According to recent reports, what about the long term value proposition of the card, though? If you fly Alaska or Hawaiian with any frequency and don’t have elite status, the basic perks add up, including a first checked bag free, preferred boarding, a quarterly lounge pass, free points sharing, and more.

    However, I’d say there’s also merit to picking up one (or both) of the personal Atmos Rewards cards….

    Sources indicate that the $395 annual fee Atmos Rewards Summit Card is the most premium Atmos Rewards credit card. While it’s a personal card, I still think it’s worth highlighting, as it’s incredibly lucrative. I’d take it a step further, and say that it’s my favorite airline credit card.

    Among other things, the card racks up status points at the fastest rate, the card allows you to earn Global Companion Awards, offers Alaska Lounge passes, enables free points sharing, waives partner award booking fees, offers 3x points on foreign purchases, and much more.

    If you fly Alaska or Hawaiian with any frequency, then getting this card is an absolute no-brainer. As I see it, the anniversary 25K-point Global Companion Award alone basically justifies the annual fee, and that claims nothing of all the other amazing perks.

    If you’re not set on an Atmos Rewards Business Card but want a dedicated business credit card that’s lucrative, there are some other great options that earn flexible points. Consider these if you want options for redeeming your rewards for more than just on Alaska, Hawaiian, and its partners:.

    The Atmos Rewards Business Card is an excellent business credit card that offers a massive welcome bonus and strong perks. The limited time welcome bonus of 90,000 Atmos Rewards points will come in handy for cardmembers, and is more than enough reason to get the card.

    In a recent development, if you don’t yet have this card and are eligible, I’d highly recommend applying. This is a card that many people don’t have, yet which offers lots of value and a great bonus.

    • “When you vote, remember a party that hates America cannot be allowed to rule over the people who built our country,” Trump remarked, referring to Democrats, whom he said want to “blow all of this up by electing communist jihadists.”.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    On the last day before the 2026 midterm elections, President Donald Trump gave a speech before the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, a site of considerable scandal in his second term. He joked it should be renamed after him and spent considerable time discussing Washington, D.C. construction projects and resurrecting conspiracy theories about monument vandals. When the president did turn to the elections, more than 23 minutes into an hour-long speech, he seemed to foreshadow major Republican losses in the House and Senate, describing it as “The most important midterm, I believe, in our lifetime.”.

    “When you vote, remember a party that hates America cannot be allowed to rule over the people who built our country,” Trump remarked, referring to Democrats, whom he said want to “blow all of this up by electing communist jihadists.”.

    Industry observers note that “If the people that voted for me and voted in the last election where we had such a great victory, if they go out and vote, just a good portion of them, we will win in a landslide,” Trump remarked midway in his speech. “Now that doesn’t happen because usually whoever the sitting president is, Republican or Democrat, uh, good or bad, good president, great president, bad, for some reason the sitting president doesn’t win the midterms, but we gave this a very strong shot.”.

    The last day of polling indicates that Democrats have odds that are better than good to flip control of the House and Senate. The final results from the New York Times/Siena University polls report “The party is ahead in all seven states likeliest to decide control of the Senate: Michigan, Kansas, Texas, Maine, Ohio and, more narrowly, Alaska and Iowa.” The final predictions in the Cook Political Report included five additional shifts for Democrats in North Carolina, Florida, Tennessee and Virginia, projecting “that Democrats will win 15 to 25 seats, putting them at a 230- to 240-seat majority.” If a sweep happens in the toss up races, it’ll give Democrats their strongest majority since 2009.

    Meanwhile, early voting records have been smashed around the country, in places like South Carolina and Ohio. In Texas, more than 7.7 million voters did so early, surpassing the record turnout for a midterm election set in 2018. Across the nation, about 50 million ballots have already been cast so far, with the share of registered Democrats notably increased in several key state races. But according to the New York Times, around half the expected votes will come on Election Day itself, making it difficult at this point to determine how major a role early votes will play in the outcome.

    Sources indicate that donald Trump just met with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping in China for a tripartite global summit — and nobody has any real news to report, except for Trump, so desperate for media attention that he’s giving interviews to anyone holding a hot mic and a video camera. The lack of news is not just because of a (predictable) blackout enforced by the Chinese Communist Party, but because the collective consciousness of America has shut down for the next few days. If you thought the traditional four-day Thanksgiving Day Weekend was typically slow, get ready for a one-and-a-half-week productivity dip in the economy as the video game Grand Theft Auto VI goes live across the nation. Even National Review, as sober-minded as it is, has more than a few fans of the series on its staff.

    Every periodical you might care to read — even the political or news-based ones — has brought forward its big-think “review” of the game, now available on PlayStation and Xbox. For all I know we’ll be publishing one too. But I am not a gamer — not in the modern sense of the word, although I did whip out my copy of Battletoads for the NES the other day to prove that I’ve still “got it” — and this will not be a review of GTA VI. Instead, I want to talk about time spent — and time wasted.

    According to recent reports, jeffrey Blehar is a National Review staff writer living in Chicago. He is also the co-host of National Review’s Political Beats podcast, which explores the great music of the modern era with guests from the political world happy to find something non-political to talk about.

    On “Grand Theft Auto VI and How We Spend Our Time”.

    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    Hill GOP looking to trim White House's $50 billion aviation ask

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (996 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy conducts a news conference on the recent nationwide ground stop after meeting with Senate Republicans in the Capitol on Tuesday.
    • Senate Republicans poured cold water Tuesday on the administration’s new ask for a $50.1 billion emergency air traffic control and airport infrastructure package, arguing much of it has little to do with the immediate problems that led to a nationwide ground stop on Friday.
    • Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought last week asked for $30.1 billion before Duffy voiced support for the rest of the funds at a Friday night press conference on the ground stop.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy conducts a news conference on the recent nationwide ground stop after meeting with Senate Republicans in the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    Senate Republicans poured cold water Tuesday on the administration’s new ask for a $50.1 billion emergency air traffic control and airport infrastructure package, arguing much of it has little to do with the immediate problems that led to a nationwide ground stop on Friday.

    Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought last week asked for $30.1 billion before Duffy voiced support for the rest of the funds at a Friday night press conference on the ground stop.

    The original ask contained roughly $12 billion that was tied directly to air traffic control upgrades, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said, with the remainder going toward long-sought airport terminal and other upgrades to aging aviation facilities.

    Duffy and Vought laid out in a letter to House and Senate appropriators on Tuesday what the extra $20 billion would be for — half for construction of five latest air route traffic control centers, and half for construction, replacement and improvement of up to 140 air traffic control towers.

    They justified the increased demand because of the “urgent need” that became evident after the ground stop. Duffy and Federal Aviation Administrator Bryan Bedford fanned out across the Capitol to try to sell the request, including a stop at Senate Republicans’ weekly policy lunch.

    But it promptly became evident that their own allies on Capitol Hill want more and better justification for why so much extra money is needed.

    Not only are there concerns that much of the request would go to terminal reconstruction and other longer-term projects, but lawmakers keep noting the FAA hasn’t yet spent about $8 billion out of the initial $12.5 billion “down payment” on air traffic control modernization provided in last year’s budget reconciliation law.

    “I don’t think the full $50 billion will be funded,” Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, noted Tuesday. “What we just discussed there, and what I expressed, is that the request needs to be focused on safety modernization.”.

    Still, Cruz said the administration had done a “good job” with the initial $12.5 billion modernization plan so far and he expected to see continued bipartisan support for the effort.

    Sources indicate that senate Republicans are considering adding additional aviation funds through a filibuster-proof reconciliation bill, a process that could begin as soon as this week with a floor “vote-a-rama” on a resolution to unlock that process. Cruz stated that while reconciliation could be the vehicle used, additional aviation funds need to be “safety-focused.”.

    Sources indicate that sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., noted after the lunch with Duffy and Bedford that he expects Congress will look at a package more in the $10 billion to $30 billion range.

    For his part, Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., said the airline industry itself should foot at least a portion of the bill, considering how much federal support the carriers have received over the years.

    Sources indicate that “I don't understand why the airline industry doesn't pay for it. We give them unbelievable amounts of money,” Scott stated, adding that he doesn’t like adding to the deficit and is “not big on government running things.”.

    Duffy explained the need for the high price tag as the result of decades of pent-up demand that are now threatening major disruptions and safety risks to the traveling public.

    According to recent reports, “This has never been done. To be clear, we are keeping planes safe in the sky, and we are switching out equipment that’s been a problem for decades,” he remarked. “I and the president have decided we are going to lean in and fix it.”.

    In a recent development, he called the effort a “historic investment” reflecting the ways air travel has changed since much of the nation’s infrastructure was built — noting that the newest tower was constructed in 1969 and much of the software being used is from the 1990s. Still, Duffy mentioned, on the current course of funding, it would take 300 years to replace every U.S. tower.

    “I'm not going to tell [Congress] how to do their work, but I'm telling everybody what we need,” Duffy remarked. “And whether it's a party-line vote or if it's a bipartisan vote, I do think this is one moment in a very charged political environment — one moment where almost all Americans and bipartisan members of both bodies are kind of in agreement that we should lean in to do this.”.

    Even as Duffy petitioned for additional funds Tuesday, he mentioned that the “root cause” of the equipment instability that made the ground stop necessary is still unclear as investigators analyze the router that caused the problem.

    A “routine switchover” from old copper wires to digital fiber in the telecommunications system “started to create challenges in our network,” Duffy explained Tuesday.

    The telecommunications transition includes the conversion of thousands of routers to what are known as Juniper devices — a process being undertaken by contractor L3Harris Technologies. Duffy and Bedford explained that 68 other routers had been converted without incident prior to the problematic switchover Friday.

    Bedford mentioned Tuesday that use of the router that officials have identified as the source of the system instability has been suspended “and we've disabled the ones that are out there.”.

    The decision to suspend use of the router followed an inquiry sent to the agency by Senate Commerce Committee Democrats a day prior. “With thousands of conversions remaining, FAA must address outstanding safety and reliability concerns before expanding installation,” they wrote.

    Bedford said he was “highly confident” that similar problems wouldn’t erupt again. “Every element of this is going to be analyzed to see what we learn here and make sure that it doesn't get repeated,” he said.

    David Jordan, Lia Chien and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

    #65450. Sacha Baron Cohen reveals “Who Is America?” and the answer is terrifying

    📅 16 Jul 2018 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1876 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Salon ↗ Open Full Page

    Sacha Baron Cohen reveals “Who Is America?” and the answer is terrifying

    📅 16 Jul 2018 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1876 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Salon

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Showtime debuted Sacha Baron Cohen’s latest series on Sunday, finally providing a partial to the question its title poses.
    • Baron Cohen bases his career on that knowledge, but watching it in action was much more entertaining two decades ago in the heyday of “Da Ali G Show.” His HBO prank show became a cultural phenomenon before the omnipresence of social media and its accelerated mainstreaming of conspiracy theory as news, before a sitting president began making the denigration of objective journalism into a sport and before the proliferation of junk science as fact.
    • Recent findings suggest that back then cameras were not so prevalent as to persuade everyone that they were only one turned corner away from stardom.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Showtime debuted Sacha Baron Cohen’s latest series on Sunday, finally providing a partial to the question its title poses. “Who Is America?” The answer, on its face, will not surprise you: we are a nation of easy marks. Not merely easy, but willing.

    Baron Cohen bases his career on that knowledge, but watching it in action was much more entertaining two decades ago in the heyday of “Da Ali G Show.” His HBO prank show became a cultural phenomenon before the omnipresence of social media and its accelerated mainstreaming of conspiracy theory as news, before a sitting president began making the denigration of objective journalism into a sport and before the proliferation of junk science as fact.

    Recent findings suggest that back then cameras were not so prevalent as to persuade everyone that they were only one turned corner away from stardom. But today, being on camera is so natural and desirable to most of us that we are willing to say or do just about anything for a few of the 15 minutes we believe to be our birthright.

    “Ali G” and the characters the show introduced, including Borat Sagdiyev and Brüno Gehard, also were born years before Project Veritas and InfoWars and other right-wing vehicles of disinformation made hidden camera hoaxing into something sinister.

    All of which is to say, “Who Is America?” is not, as Showtime would like you to believe, “the most dangerous show in history.” At best, it is an occasionally funny one.

    Recent findings suggest that but to anyone who mourns the collective deterioration of our population’s capacity to engage in critical thought, but has no idea of how urgent of a crisis that happens to be, Baron Cohen’s new endeavor is less of a comedy than a fright show. “Who Is America?” A nation of pliable dullards ripe for the hacking.

    “Who Is America?” was produced in secret, and its pre-show marketing largely consisted of publicized declarations of outrage by such right-wing figures as Joe Walsh, Sarah Palin and Roy Moore. Each attempted to transform their extreme embarrassment at having been duped by a British clown hiding behind layers of latex and spirit gum into some approximation of righteous anger at said comedian’s dishonesty.

    It has been revealed that showtime, meanwhile, maintained the aura of mystery surrounding the series almost to the brink of its debut, revealing the title only a little more than a week prior. The network released the briefest of clips featuring one famous interview subject, Dick Cheney.

    This in itself was a bit of flimflam Showtime’s part: “Hope you’ll tune in next week for an interview with me,” Cheney indicates in the video, only to be a no-show in the premiere.

    Sources indicate that you can’t blame “Who Is America?” for saving its biggest fish for later, because the famous politicians in the opener prove the problem of our collective gullibility just fine by themselves. In fact, although liberals may have gotten a hearty guffaw out of hearing Palin’s wailing about having been faked out by Baron Cohen, the very same character — Dr. Billy Wayne Ruddick Jr. PhD of Truthbrary.org — sat down for a conversation with none other than the honorable junior senator from Vermont, Bernie Sanders.

    Sources indicate that prior to the premiere Billy Wayne tweeted a response to Palin’s accusation that he made fun disabled veterans. “I did NOT say I was a War Vet,” Ruddick’s “official” response reads, going on to explain that the service was in was “not military, but United Parcel”.

    In a recent development, nor does he make such assertions to Sanders, with whom he debates the merits of a universal healthcare strategy. And when I say debate, what I mean is that Sanders very calmly shares statistics with Billy Wayne long after the interviewer’s line of questioning stops making sense. And when Sanders asks Billy Wayne to confirm that he is disabled, given that he is conducting the interview while seated on a motorized scooter, Baron Cohen’s character replies that no, he is not. “This here scooter is to preserve my body’s finite energy,” Billy Wayne says.

    READ MORE: That viral “strangers on a plane” Twitter story: Not a rom-com but a horror show.

    One may be tempted to qualify Sanders’ appearance by pointing out that he acquitted himself well in the face of a person best be described as a few coconuts short of a beach vacation in Binomo.

    Industry observers note that but this fails to answer the question of why Sanders signed a release, allowing this interview to be broadcast. Did anyone on Sanders’ team vet Truthbrary.org the moment Billy Wayne mentioned it? Even if they thought he was genuine, what is to be gained from being seen in a televised debate with a guy whose site includes a page titled  “Obamanoids — For Real!”?

    (To be fair, reportedly Baron Cohen almost fooled veteran news anchor Ted Koppel as part of his project. Koppel told The Hollywood Reporter that he was contacted to appear in a Showtime project titled “Age of Reason,” said to feature “conversations with distinguished experts in science and public policy, highlighting the brightest and most reputable minds on today’s most important topics.” Koppel, perhaps receiving brainwaves from his colleague Sam Donaldson, wised up before Baron Cohen could pull him too deeply into his game.).

    A second character introduced in the premiere, an NPR shirt-wearing hyper-liberal named  Nira Cain-N’Degeocello, visits the opulent South Carolina home of wealthy Trump supporters he notes are  “afflicted with white privilege.” But it soon becomes clear that his marks’ problem isn’t close-mindedness but over-correcting in the acceptance department. When Baron Cohen’s interviewer waxes on about encouraging his daughter Malala to “free bleed” on the American flag as a lesson, they simply nod and listen; when he chats about his wife’s ongoing affair with a dolphin, they don’t have any questions like, say, whether what they’re hearing is real.

    This brings us to another answer to “Who Is America?”: we’re so aware of cameras, and desperate to have its focus upon us, that we will do and say anything without thinking of its possible permanence.

    Demonstrating this is Baron Cohen’s third character Rick Sherman, an ex-con turned TV host who visits a Laguna Beach, California gallery to show his work, which is a series of capable but otherwise unextraordinary portraits rendered in feces and ejaculate.

    Sources indicate that now, it’s entirely possible that the woman who runs the gallery might have been thinking she could have the next Andres Serrano on her hands. On the other hand, please.

    This is a subject entirely aware of being on view, so obsessed with appearing erudite that while Rick is off camera, having excused himself to the facilities to commit another brown-and-white vision to paper, she addresses the camera like the host she was born to be.

    According to recent reports, “Who knew the world was capable of such oxymoronic paradoxical juxtapositions?” she muses. And this is before the homemade pubic hair paintbrush comes out.

    Baron Cohen has pushed the limits of tolerant everyday people many times in the past, mostly in a way that makes them look reasonable or, at the very least, more intelligent than the put-ons he inflicts upon them. And this is perhaps one of the most depressing aspects about “Who Is America?”, its demonstration of how endemic our lack of analysis truly is. I’m not saying that gallery owner is a stupid woman, understand.

    Recent findings suggest that but her interview is an example of prizing exposure over lasting consequence. By that I’m not merely referring to the fact that she placated a man who not only handed her pieces of cardboard purportedly smeared with his own dried excrement, or waited to receive a fresh sample of his work, but that she decided she needed to share her expert observation as to why she needed to do so by uttering a sentence full of five dollar words that add up to absolute nonsense.

    Recent findings suggest that (Either that or she’s a friend of Baron Cohen’s and in on the gag. I hope it’s option two, as opposed to her actually legitimizing the artistic relevance of number two.).

    A number of reviews of “Who Is America?” have pointed out that Baron Cohen’s sneaky deceit is no longer funny because the formerly insane viewpoints Baron Cohen’s tactics expose have been normalized.

    In a recent development, this has always been the danger, but it’s one every sort of parody or satire contends with in the current climate. It’s difficult to lampoon leaders seeking to legislate ludicrous patches to crises like gun violence instead of adopting common sense solutions like stricter regulation.

    Which brings us to the portion of “Who Is America?” guaranteed to dominate Monday’s gallery of crazy clips, fronted by Baron Cohen’s Col. Erran Morad, a self-styled Israeli anti-terrorism expert who calls himself “the terrorist terminator.”.

    The fake Mossad officer is there to promote his “Kinderguardians” program, a proposal that aims to train and arm toddlers in the classroom because, Moran indicates, arming teachers is crazy.

    In a recent development, and this is the portion that has Walsh’s boxers in a bunch, because he joins House representatives Dana Rohrabacher and Joe Wilson in lending on-camera endorsements. Walsh’s comments are interwoven with a series of fake testimonials from the likes of Larry Pratt, executive director emeritus of the lobbying group Gun Owners of America and rape joke enthusiast.

    According to recent reports, nobody forced Walsh to say, with gusto, “The way to stop a bad guy with is a good child with a gun. Happy shooting, kids!” If he didn’t want to say it, he wouldn’t have.

    What Walsh might be upset about is being upstaged by Pratt, who earns some of the episode’s biggest laughs by reading the “science” behind the effectiveness of the fake program, revealing he doesn’t know the difference between human anatomy and hitmakers who grace Billboard’s pop charts.

    Yes, “Who Is America?” gets mileage out of highlighting the callousness, sexism and extraordinary gullibility of conservatives, as Baron Cohen always has. But the things they say to him in disguise aren’t all that different than what they’d say on CNN, Fox, MSNBC or talk radio. Whatever power his comedy used to reveal is diminished by the fact that the charlatans no longer operate in secret.

    Next week’s episode introduces one or two fresh characters, although I don’t imagine they do anything more “dangerous” than the four we met on Sunday. For a number of viewers who love Baron Cohen’s schtick, that won’t matter.

    To them “Who Is America?” is precisely on brand, showing Americans famous and everyday reacting to bizarre situations with varying degrees of what we consider to be normalcy in a time where the baseline version of normal is constantly morphing and shifting.

    Recent findings suggest that to other viewers, however, “Who Is America?” is a confirmation that Baron Cohen has run some tests and can confirm there is limited and ever decreasing brain activity in this worsening patient we know as America. It is something to behold, that’s for sure. But I’m not sure it’s the stuff of groundbreaking comedy. It’s not even really news.
